Conversely, independent variables with finite variances are uncorrelated, so @thm-qf-mean-var(c) gives 2\B Sigma\A mu= zero for every  mu, that is, \B Sigma\A= m0. [Two quadratic forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A,\B be symmetric. If \A Sigma\B= m0, equivalently \B Sigma\A= m0, then \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent. The two conditions are transposes of each other. As before, \A\Y and \B\Y are jointly normal with \Cov(\A\Y,\B\Y)=\A Sigma\B= m0, hence independent, and each form is a function of one of them. The condition is sufficient for every  mu and every  Sigma. When  Sigma is singular one might hope that the weaker requirement  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma= m0 suffices, since only directions in \C( Sigma) carry noise. For nonnegative definite \A and \B the two requirements turn out to be equivalent (@exr-qf-singular-independence). In the other direction, the condition is necessary under mild assumptions, a result usually credited to Craig (1943). Its general proof is surprisingly delicate, and the history of incorrect published proofs is recounted by Driscoll and Gundberg (1986). The case that matters most for sums of squares has a short proof. [Necessity for nonnegative definite forms] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero,\I) and let \A,\B be nonnegative definite. If \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent, then \A\B= m0. Independence makes the covariance zero, and by @thm-qf-mean-var(d) the covariance is 2	r(\A\B). With the square roots of @thm-mat-square-root, 	r(\A\B)=	r(\A^{1/2}\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}\B^{1/2})=	r igl\{(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2})\T(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}) igr\}, the sum of squares of the entries of \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}. So \A^{1/2}\B^{1/2}= m0, and \A\B=\A^{1/2}(\A^{1/2}\B^{1/2})\B^{1/2}= m0. For nonnegative definite forms in a standard normal vector, then, zero correlation and independence coincide, just as for jointly normal linear forms. This fails for general symmetric matrices (@exr-qf-uncorrelated-dependent). Orthogonal projections of a spherical normal vector The situation in regression is the tidiest one: a spherical normal vector and several projections onto mutually orthogonal subspaces. [Independent projections] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let  P_1,\dots, P_k be symmetric idempotent matrices with  P_i P_j= m0 for i
e j, and ranks r_1,\dots,r_k. Then  P_1\Y,\dots, P_k\Y are mutually independent normal vectors,  P_i\Y\sim\Normal_n( P_i mu,\sigma^2 P_i), and the sums of squares  rac{
orm{ P_i\Y}^2}{\sigma^2}\sim\chi^2\Bigl(r_i, rac{
orm{ P_i mu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), \qquad i=1,\dots,k, are mutually independent. Stack the vectors  P_i\Y into one nk-vector. It is a linear function of \Y, so it is normal, and the covariance between blocks i and j is  P_i(\sigma^2\I) P_j\T=\sigma^2 P_i P_j. This is  m 0 for i
e j and \sigma^2 P_i for i=j. By the block form of @thm-mvn-independence the blocks are mutually independent, and functions of them, the squared lengths, are then mutually independent. Their laws are @thm-qf-chisq(a). In geometric language, which Chapter 6 develops: the coordinates of a spherical normal vector in mutually orthogonal subspaces are independent. It is the reason the rows of an analysis of variance table can be treated separately. [Sample mean and sample variance] Let Y_1,\dots,Y_n (n\ge2) be independent \Normal(\mu,\sigma^2), with sample mean  ar{Y} and sample variance S^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i- ar{Y})^2. Then 1.  ar{Y} and S^2 are independent, and  ar{Y}\sim\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2/n); 2. (n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1); 3. for any \mu_0, T=\sqrt n( ar{Y}-\mu_0)/S\sim t(n-1,\delta) with \delta=\sqrt n(\mu-\mu_0)/\sigma. In particular T\sim t(n-1) when \mu=\mu_0. Here \Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu one,\sigma^2\I). Let  P_1=n^{-1} one one\T and  m C=\I- P_1. Both are symmetric and idempotent,  P_1 m C= m0, and ank( m C)=	r( m C)=n-1. Since  P_1\Y= ar{Y} one and 
orm{ m C\Y}^2=(n-1)S^2, @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections gives (a), which @exm-mvn-mean-deviations obtained directly, and, because  m C\mu one= zero, also (b). For (c), X=\sqrt n( ar{Y}-\mu_0)/\sigma\sim\Normal(\delta,1) and V=(n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1) are independent, and T=X/\sqrt{V/(n-1)}. Apply @def-qf-noncentral-t. The independence in (a) characterizes the normal distribution: for n\ge2 independent identically distributed observations with finite variance,  ar{Y} and S^2 are independent only under normality (Lukacs 1942). We will not need this, but it shows that normality is used essentially here. It is not a technicality that more careful arguments could remove. Preview: the F statistic for nested models The main use of these results comes in Chapter 11. Its core fits in a few lines. [F statistic for nested subspaces] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let  P_0 and  P be symmetric idempotent matrices of ranks r_0<r<n with  P P_0= P_0. Suppose that  P mu= mu. Then F= rac{\Y\T( P- P_0)\Y/(r-r_0)}{\Y\T(\I- P)\Y/(n-r)} \sim F\Bigl(r-r_0,\;n-r,\; rac{
orm{( P- P_0) mu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), and the noncentrality is zero iff  P_0 mu= mu. Transposing  P P_0= P_0 gives  P_0 P= P_0. Hence ( P- P_0)^2= P-2 P_0+ P_0= P- P_0, so  P- P_0 is symmetric idempotent with rank 	r( P)-	r( P_0)=r-r_0. Also ( P- P_0)(\I- P)= P- P- P_0+ P_0= m0, and \I- P is symmetric idempotent of rank n-r. By @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections the numerator and denominator sums of squares are independent, with \sigma^{-2} times them distributed as \chi^2(r-r_0,
orm{( P- P_0) mu}^2/\sigma^2) and \chi^2(n-r,
orm{(\I- P) mu}^2/\sigma^2). The second noncentrality is 0 since  P mu= mu. The unknown \sigma^2 cancels in the ratio, and @def-qf-noncentral-f applies. Finally, ( P- P_0) mu= mu- P_0 mu. In a linear model,  P=\M projects onto the column space of the full model matrix \X and  P_0=\Mo onto that of a submodel \X_0. The numerator is the drop in residual sum of squares from the submodel to the full model (Chapter 6). The theorem says three things. The test that rejects for large F has an exactly known null distribution. Its power depends on the unknown parameters only through \gamma=
orm{(\M-\Mo)\X beta}^2/\sigma^2. And, by @thm-qf-f-power, that power increases with \gamma. [Detecting curvature] Let x_1,\dots,x_n, n=15, be equally spaced on [0,1], and suppose Y_i=1+0.5x_i+ eta_2x_i^2+\varepsilon_i with independent \Normal(0,1) errors. To test for curvature, compare the straight line (\X_0=[ one,\x]) with the quadratic (\X=[ one,\x,\x^2]). The F statistic has 1 and 12 degrees of freedom, and the 5\% critical value is 4.747. For  eta_2=8.0, the listing finds \gamma=6.873 and power 0.673 from the noncentral F, and the rejection rate in 100{,}000 simulated data sets is 0.674. The noncentrality has a clear meaning. It is  eta_2^2 times the squared length of the part of \x^2 orthogonal to  one and \x, divided by \sigma^2. It grows roughly in proportion to n for a fixed design pattern. Keeping the same design on [0,1], the smallest n with power at least 0.8 is 21, where \gamma=8.97. Figure 4.4.1 places the example on the power curve and shows the loss of power when the same noncentrality is spread over more numerator degrees of freedom r. At \gamma=10 the power is 0.827, 0.606 and 0.421 for r=1,3,6. import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(1104) alpha, s = 0.05, 12 def power(gamma, q, s, alpha=0.05): crit = stats.f.ppf(1 - alpha, q, s) return stats.ncf.sf(crit, q, s, np.maximum(gamma, 1e-12)) gammas = np.linspace(0, 30, 301) gamma_ref, rs = 10.0, (1, 3, 6) # r = numerator degrees of freedom curves = {q: power(gammas, q, s) for q in rs} n, sigma, beta0, beta1, beta2, reps = 15, 1.0, 1.0, 0.5, 8.0, 100_000 x = np.linspace(0, 1, n) X0 = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x]) # straight line X = np.column_stack([X0, x**2]) # adds curvature def proj(Z): Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(Z) return Q @ Q.T M, M0 = proj(X), proj(X0) mean = X @ np.array([beta0, beta1, beta2]) gamma = mean @ (M - M0) @ mean / sigma**2 # noncentrality q, df_resid = 1, n - 3 crit = stats.f.ppf(0.95, q, df_resid) exact_power = stats.ncf.sf(crit, q, df_resid, gamma) Y = mean + sigma * rng.standard_normal((reps, n)) num = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, M - M0, Y) / q den = np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, np.eye(n) - M, Y) / df_resid print(gamma, exact_power, np.mean(num / den > crit)) [Figure 4.4.1. Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature.] Figure 4.4.1. Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature. [Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature.] Power \Pr\{F(r,12,\gamma)>F_{0.05}(r,12)\} of the level-0.05 F test as a function of the noncentrality. Every curve starts at 0.05 and increases to 1 (@thm-qf-f-power). For a fixed \gamma, power falls as the number r of numerator degrees of freedom grows. The dot is the curvature test of @exm-qf-curvature. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] In @exm-qf-drift let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu one,\sigma^2\I) with n\ge3. Use @thm-qf-mean-var(d) to show that \Cov(S^2,Q)=\Var(S^2), and deduce that S^2 and Q are dependent with correlation \{2(n-1)/(3n-4)\}^{1/2}. Which linear forms  m a\T\Y are independent of Q for every mean vector  mu\in\Real^n? With  Sigma=\sigma^2\I, part (d) of @thm-qf-mean-var gives \Cov(S^2,Q)=2\sigma^4	r( m C D\T D)/\{2(n-1)^2\}. Since  D one= zero,  m C D\T D= D\T D, whose trace is 2(n-1), so \Cov(S^2,Q)=2\sigma^4/(n-1)=\Var(S^2). The mean terms vanish because  m C mu= D mu= zero. Using \Var(Q) from @exm-qf-drift-variance, the correlation is \{\Var(S^2)/\Var(Q)\}^{1/2}=\{2(n-1)/(3n-4)\}^{1/2}, which is nonzero, so the forms are dependent. By @thm-qf-indep-linear,  m a\T\Y is independent of Q for every  mu iff  m a\T D\T D= zero\T. Multiplying by  m a gives 
orm{ D m a}^2=0, so  D m a= zero and  m a is a multiple of  one; conversely such  m a work. The only such linear forms are the multiples of  ar{Y}. B. Practice [B1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_2( zero,\I). Show that Y_1^2-Y_2^2 and 2Y_1Y_2 are uncorrelated but not independent. Why does @prp-qf-craig-nnd not apply? With \A=\diag(1,-1) and \B= egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}, 	r(\A\B)=0, so the covariance 2	r(\A\B) is zero. In polar coordinates Y_1=R\cos\Theta, Y_2=R\sin\Theta, with R^2\sim\chi^2(2) independent of \Theta uniform on [0,2\pi), the two forms are R^2\cos2\Theta and R^2\sin2\Theta. Now \E(R^4)=8 and \E(R^8)=384, so \E[(R^2\cos2\Theta)^2(R^2\sin2\Theta)^2]=384/8=48, but the product of the expected squares is (8/2)^2=16. The forms are dependent. @prp-qf-craig-nnd needs nonnegative definite matrices, and \A and \B are indefinite. [B2] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu, Sigma) and let \A,\B be nonnegative definite with  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma= m0. Show that \A Sigma\B= m0, so that \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent. Show by an example that the implication can fail when \A is not nonnegative definite. Write \A=\R\R\T and \B= S S\T, for instance with symmetric square roots, and  Sigma= L L\T with  L of full column rank. Cancelling  L on both sides of  L( L\T\A L)( L\T\B L) L\T= m0 gives  L\T\A L L\T\B L= m0. The trace of this matrix is 	r( L\T\R\R\T L L\T S S\T L)=	r\{(\R\T Sigma S)(\R\T Sigma S)\T\}=
orm{\R\T Sigma S}_F^2, so \R\T Sigma S= m0. Hence \A Sigma\B=\R(\R\T Sigma S) S\T= m0, and @thm-qf-indep-quadratic applies. For nonnegative definite matrices the two conditions are therefore equivalent, since \A Sigma\B= m0 trivially implies  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma= m0. Without nonnegative definiteness the argument breaks at the trace step. Take  Sigma=\diag(1,0), \A= egin{psmallmatrix}0&1\1&0\end{psmallmatrix} and \B=\I_2. Then  Sigma\A Sigma= m0, so  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma= m0, but \A Sigma\B= egin{psmallmatrix}0&0\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}
e m0. With  mu=(0,m)\T and m
e0 we have Y_2=m with probability one, so the forms are 2mY_1 and Y_1^2+m^2. The second is a nonconstant function of the first, so they are dependent. [B3] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n(\X beta,\sigma^2\I) with \X of full column rank p<n, let \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y, \M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T and s^2=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/(n-p). With v_{jj} the jth diagonal entry of (\X\T\X)^{-1}, show that (\hat{ eta}_j-b)/(s\sqrt{v_{jj}})\sim t igl(n-p,( eta_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}) igr). Here \M is symmetric and idempotent with 	r\M=	r\{(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\X\}=p, and \M\X=\X. So (n-p)s^2/\sigma^2=
orm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-p) by @thm-qf-chisq(a), because (\I-\M)\X beta= zero. With \B=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T, \B(\sigma^2\I)(\I-\M)=\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}(\X\T-\X\T\M)= m0, so \hbeta=\B\Y is independent of s^2 (@thm-qf-indep-linear). Since \hbeta\sim\Normal_p( beta,\sigma^2(\X\T\X)^{-1}), the variable X=(\hat{ eta}_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}) is \Normal igl(( eta_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}}),1 igr). The statistic is X/\sqrt{V/(n-p)} with V=(n-p)s^2/\sigma^2, and @def-qf-noncentral-t applies. [B4] Show that F_\alpha(r,s)	o\chi^2_\alpha(r)/r as s	o\infty, where \chi^2_\alpha(r) is the upper \alpha point of \chi^2(r), and that the power \Pr\{F(r,s,\gamma)>F_\alpha(r,s)\} tends to \Pr\{\chi^2(r,\gamma)>\chi^2_\alpha(r)\}, the power of the test that knows \sigma^2.

title: 4.5 The Cochran theorem
content:
The Cochran theorem An analysis of variance starts from an identity \Y\T\Y=\Y\T\A_1\Y+\dots+\Y\T\A_k\Y,\qquad \A_1+\dots+\A_k=\I, that splits the total sum of squares into pieces attributed to sources of variation. @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections says the pieces are independent chi-squared variables when the \A_i are mutually orthogonal projections. Checking that directly means checking k idempotence conditions and  inom k2 orthogonality conditions. Cochran’s theorem shows that one count of ranks does all of it. The algebra The matrix algebra behind this was done in Chapter 1. For symmetric matrices, any two of the three properties “each \A_i is idempotent”, “\A_i\A_j= m0 for i
e j” and “the sum is idempotent” imply the third, and symmetric matrices that add to \I with ranks adding to n are idempotent and mutually orthogonal (@thm-mat-idempotent-sum). The next theorem adds the rank count for a sum that is idempotent but not necessarily \I, which is what nested models need. [Cochran, algebraic form] Let \A_1,\dots,\A_k be symmetric n	imes n matrices and \A=\sum_i\A_i. Consider 1. each \A_i is idempotent; 2. \A_i\A_j= m0 for all i
e j; 3. \A is idempotent; 4. ank(\A)=\sum_iank(\A_i). Then any two of (a), (b), (c) imply all four, and (c) together with (d) implies all four. Any two of (a), (b), (c). By @thm-mat-idempotent-sum, any two of them imply the third. When all three hold, rank equals trace for symmetric idempotent matrices (@thm-mat-idempotent), so ank(\A)=	r(\A)=\sum_i	r(\A_i)=\sum_iank(\A_i), which is (d). (c) and (d) imply (a) and (b). Let r=ank(\A) and r_i=ank(\A_i). Every \A v=\sum_i\A_i v lies in \C(\A_1)+\dots+\C(\A_k), whose dimension is at most \sum_ir_i=r=\dim\C(\A). So the two spaces coincide, and in particular \C(\A_i)\subseteq\C(\A). By @thm-mat-idempotent(a), \A=\Q\Q\T with \Q of size n	imes r and \Q\T\Q=\I_r. Since \A is symmetric and idempotent it fixes every vector of its column space, so \A\A_i=\A_i, and transposing, \A_i\A=\A_i. Hence \A_i=\A\A_i\A=\Q\B_i\Q\T with \B_i=\Q\T\A_i\Q. The r	imes r matrices \B_i are symmetric, satisfy \sum_i\B_i=\Q\T\A\Q=\I_r, and have ank(\B_i)=r_i because \Q has orthonormal columns. By the last statement of @thm-mat-idempotent-sum, \B_i^2=\B_i and \B_i\B_j= m0 for i
e j, and multiplying by \Q on the left and \Q\T on the right transfers both identities to the \A_i. The distributional statement [Cochran] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I), and let \A_1,\dots,\A_k be symmetric with ranks r_1,\dots,r_k, whose sum \A=\sum_i\A_i is idempotent of rank r (for example \A=\I, r=n). The following are equivalent: 1. the forms \Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2 are mutually independent, and \Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(r_i, mu\T\A_i mu/\sigma^2) for each i; 2. r_1+\dots+r_k=r; 3. each \A_i is idempotent; 4. \A_i\A_j= m0 for all i
e j. Condition (c) of @thm-qf-cochran-algebra holds by assumption, so that theorem shows that (ii), (iii) and (iv) are equivalent, and each implies the other two. If (iii) and (iv) hold, @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections gives (i). If (i) holds, apply @thm-qf-chisq-identity to \sigma^{-1}\Y\sim\Normal_n(\sigma^{-1} mu,\I). Each \A_i with r_i\ge1 is idempotent, and an \A_i of rank zero is  m0. This is (iii). In words: if the degrees of freedom add up, the sums of squares are independent chi-squared variables. Independence in (i) is not needed to reach (iii). The marginal chi-squared laws alone force the whole structure. [The one-way layout] Let observations fall into g groups of sizes n_1,\dots,n_g, with Y_{\ell j} independent \Normal(\mu_\ell,\sigma^2). Let \M replace each observation by its group mean, and  P_1=n^{-1} one one\T by the grand mean. Then \I= P_1+(\M- P_1)+(\I-\M) splits 
orm{\Y}^2 into n ar{Y}^2, the between-group sum of squares \sum_\ell n_\ell( ar{Y}_\ell- ar{Y})^2 and the within-group sum of squares \sum_{\ell,j}(Y_{\ell j}- ar{Y}_\ell)^2. The three matrices are symmetric with ranks 1, g-1 and n-g, which add to n. Cochran’s theorem needs nothing more. The three sums of squares, divided by \sigma^2, are independent noncentral chi-squared variables. Their noncentralities are n ar{\mu}^2/\sigma^2, \sum_\ell n_\ell(\mu_\ell- ar{\mu})^2/\sigma^2 with  ar{\mu}=\sum_\ell n_\ell\mu_\ell/n, and 0. The last is zero because \M mu= mu. The ratio of the between and within mean squares is F(g-1,n-g,\gamma) by @thm-qf-nested-f, and it is central iff all group means are equal. The script uses g=3 groups of sizes 3, 5, 4, means 2, 3, 1.5, and \sigma=1, and draws 200{,}000 data sets. Table 4.5.1 compares the theoretical means r_i+\gamma_i and variances 2r_i+4\gamma_i with the simulated ones. The largest absolute correlation between the three sums of squares is 0.0013. As a check that goes beyond correlation, the proportion of data sets in which both the between and the within sums of squares exceed their medians is 0.2497, against 0.25 for independent variables. import numpy as np from scipy import stats rng = np.random.default_rng(5150) sizes, means, sigma = [3, 5, 4], [2.0, 3.0, 1.5], 1.0 groups = np.repeat(np.arange(3), sizes) n = len(groups) Z = (groups[:, None] == np.arange(3)).astype(float) # group indicators M = Z @ np.diag(1 / np.array(sizes)) @ Z.T # group-mean projection J = np.ones((n, n)) / n pieces = [J, M - J, np.eye(n) - M] ranks = [np.linalg.matrix_rank(P) for P in pieces] print("ranks", ranks, "sum", sum(ranks), "n", n) mu = np.array(means)[groups] gammas = [mu @ P @ mu / sigma**2 for P in pieces] Y = mu + sigma * rng.standard_normal((200_000, n)) Q = np.stack([np.einsum("ij,jk,ik->i", Y, P, Y) for P in pieces], axis=1) / sigma**2 print(np.corrcoef(Q, rowvar=False).round(3)) Table 4.5.1. Cochran decomposition for a one-way layout with n=12: theory against 200{,}000 simulated data sets. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Sum of squares r_i \gamma_i mean simulated variance simulated ---------------- ---------- ---------- ---------- ----------- ---------- ----------- grand mean 1 60.750 61.750 61.763 245.00 244.95 between groups 2 5.250 7.250 7.230 25.00 24.85 within groups 9 0.000 9.000 8.994 18.00 17.96 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ [What the theorem does not cover] Two assumptions carry the weight. The first is normality. Without it, @thm-qf-mean-var(d) fails, and with independent non-normal errors the between and within sums of squares are in general correlated, with a correlation driven by the fourth cumulant (@exr-qf-kurtosis). The second is the spherical covariance \sigma^2\I. With \Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\V, \V positive definite, apply the theorem to \V^{-1/2}\Y, whose forms have matrices \V^{1/2}\A_i\V^{1/2}. Their ranks are those of the \A_i, so the rank count is unchanged. What changes is the condition on the sum: \V^{1/2}\A\V^{1/2} is idempotent iff \A\V\A=\A (for example \sum_i\A_i=\V^{-1}), and conditions (iii) and (iv) become \A_i\V\A_i=\A_i and \A_i\V\A_j= m0. These are the generalized least squares decompositions of Chapter 31. Most analysis of variance tables in this book come from a chain of nested model spaces. The successive differences of their projections are mutually orthogonal projections whose ranks add up, so Cochran’s theorem applies without further work (@exr-qf-sequential, Chapter 9). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \A_1=\diag(2,0) and \A_2=\diag(-1,1), so that \A_1+\A_2=\I_2. Which hypotheses of @thm-qf-cochran fail, and what are the laws of the two forms when \Y\sim\Normal_2( zero,\I)? The sum \I_2 is idempotent, but every one of the conditions (ii)–(iv) fails. The ranks are 1 and 2, which add to 3
e2. Neither matrix is idempotent, since \A_1^2=\diag(4,0) and \A_2^2=\I_2. And \A_1\A_2=\diag(-2,0)
e m0. The forms are 2Y_1^2, which is twice a \chi^2(1) variable, and Y_2^2-Y_1^2, the difference of two independent \chi^2(1) variables, which takes negative values. Neither is chi-squared. They are dependent, because \Cov(2Y_1^2,\,Y_2^2-Y_1^2)=2\Cov(Y_1^2,Y_2^2)-2\Var(Y_1^2)=0-2\cdot2=-4
e0 . B. Practice [B1] A two-way layout has one observation Y_{ij} for each of a rows and b columns. Write 
orm{\Y}^2 as the sum of the grand-mean, row, column and residual sums of squares, identify the four matrices, and use @thm-qf-cochran to show that under Y_{ij}\sim\Normal(\mu+\alpha_i+ eta_j,\sigma^2) independently the four sums of squares are independent, with degrees of freedom 1, a-1, b-1 and (a-1)(b-1). [B2] Let  P_1,\dots, P_m be symmetric idempotent with \C( P_1)\subset\C( P_2)\subset\dots\subset\C( P_m), and put  P_0= m0,  P_{m+1}=\I. Show that the matrices  P_i- P_{i-1}, i=1,\dots,m+1, satisfy the conditions of @thm-qf-cochran, so that the sequential sums of squares 
orm{( P_i- P_{i-1})\Y}^2 are independent noncentral chi-squared variables when \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\sigma^2\I). C. Going deeper [C1] Let \Y\sim\Normal_n( zero,\I), and Q=Q_1+Q_2 with Q=\Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r), Q_1=\Y\T\A_1\Y\sim\chi^2(r_1) and Q_2=\Y\T\A_2\Y for a nonnegative definite \A_2. Show that Q_1 and Q_2 are independent and Q_2\sim\chi^2(r-r_1). By @thm-qf-chisq-identity, \A and \A_1 are idempotent, with ranks r and r_1. If \A v= zero, then 0= v\T\A_1 v+ v\T\A_2 v with both terms nonnegative, so 
orm{\A_1 v}^2= v\T\A_1 v=0. Thus \Null(\A)\subseteq\Null(\A_1), hence \C(\A_1)\subseteq\C(\A) and \A\A_1=\A_1=\A_1\A. Then \A_2^2=(\A-\A_1)^2=\A-2\A_1+\A_1=\A_2, so \A_2 is idempotent, and \A_1\A_2=\A_1\A-\A_1= m0. By @thm-qf-orthogonal-projections, Q_1 and Q_2 are independent and Q_2\sim\chi^2(	r\A_2)=\chi^2(r-r_1).

title: 4.6 Summary and Notes
content:
Summary and Notes Summary 1. If \Z\sim\Normal_r( mu,\I) then 
orm{\Z}^2\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma) with \gamma=
orm{ mu}^2, mean r+\gamma and variance 2r+4\gamma. The law is a Poisson(\gamma/2) mixture of \chi^2(r+2k) laws, and its tails increase strictly with \gamma (@thm-qf-ncchisq and @prp-qf-ncchisq-monotone). 2. F(r,s,\gamma) and t(s,\delta) put a noncentral numerator over an independent central denominator. The power of an F test increases strictly with \gamma, and T^2\sim F(1,s,\delta^2) (@thm-qf-f-power). 3. \E(\Y\T\A\Y)=	r(\A Sigma)+ mu\T\A mu for any distribution. Under normality \Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2	r\{(\A Sigma)^2\}+4 mu\T\A Sigma\A mu,\qquad \Cov( m K\Y,\Y\T\A\Y)=2 m K Sigma\A mu (@thm-qf-mean-var). 4. A normal quadratic form is a constant plus independent terms \lambda_j(W_j+
u_j)^2, and for singular  Sigma possibly normal terms. The weights \lambda_j are the nonzero eigenvalues of \A Sigma (@thm-qf-canonical). 5. For \Y\sim\Normal_n( mu,\I), \Y\T\A\Y is chi-squared iff \A is idempotent. Then the degrees of freedom are ank\A=	r\A and the noncentrality is  mu\T\A mu (@thm-qf-chisq-identity). For positive definite  Sigma the condition is that \A Sigma be idempotent. For projections, 
orm{ P\Y}^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(ank P,
orm{ P mu}^2/\sigma^2) (@thm-qf-chisq). 6. \B\Y and \Y\T\A\Y are independent if \B Sigma\A= m0, and \Y\T\A\Y and \Y\T\B\Y are independent if \A Sigma\B= m0, because a quadratic form is a function of \A\Y (@thm-qf-indep-linear and @thm-qf-indep-quadratic). 7. Projections of a spherical normal vector onto mutually orthogonal subspaces are independent. This gives the independence of  ar{Y} and S^2 and the exact F(r-r_0,n-r,\gamma) law of the nested-model F statistic (@thm-qf-orthogonal-projections, @cor-qf-sample-variance and @thm-qf-nested-f). 8. Cochran: if symmetric matrices add to an idempotent matrix and their ranks add up, the corresponding sums of squares are independent chi-squared variables (@thm-qf-cochran-algebra and @thm-qf-cochran). Notes and sources Source texts. Rencher and Schaalje (2008, chapter 5) cover the material of Section 4.2, Section 4.3, Section 4.4 and Section 4.5 for positive definite covariance matrices. They derive the mgf of a quadratic form by integrating against the normal density and obtain its variance by differentiating the logarithm of the mgf; the converse of the chi-squared theorem is referred to the literature. They use the noncentrality  mu\T mu/2. Seber and Lee (2003, section 2.4) reduce the general case to a spherical normal vector by an orthogonal diagonalization. They prove necessity of idempotence for central forms by factorizing the moment generating function, and give the eigenvalue criterion for singular covariance matrices. Christensen (2020, section 1.3) states the three conditions of @thm-qf-chisq(c) for arbitrary nonnegative definite  Sigma, and obtains independence by viewing quadratic forms as functions of linear ones, the approach followed in Section 4.4. The canonical representation (@thm-qf-canonical), the proof of necessity through the coefficients @eq-qf-cumulant-match, the monotonicity proof through the Poisson mixture, and the treatment of the Cochran algebra are this book’s own arrangements of standard material. Noncentral distributions. The noncentral chi-squared distribution first appeared in Fisher (1928). Patnaik (1949) studied its approximation by a scaled central chi-squared variable, and Satterthwaite (1946) used the same two-moment idea for linear combinations of mean squares, which reappears in Chapter 32. Johnson et al. (1995, chapters 29–31) collect the properties of the noncentral chi-squared, F and t families. The monotonicity of power in the noncentrality and in the degrees of freedom is treated systematically by Ghosh (1973). General quadratic forms. The exact distribution of a quadratic form that is not chi-squared can be computed by numerical inversion of its characteristic function (Gil-Pelaez 1951; Imhof 1961). Mathai and Provost (1992) give a book-length treatment of quadratic forms in normal and non-normal variables. The mean square successive difference of @exm-qf-drift goes back to von Neumann (1941), who derived the exact distribution of its ratio to S^2. Independence and Cochran’s theorem. Cochran (1934) proved the decomposition theorem that bears his name, in the context of the analysis of covariance. The necessity of \A Sigma\B= m0 for independence of two forms is attributed to Craig (1943). Its full proof for arbitrary symmetric matrices and arbitrary means turned out to be subtle, and Driscoll and Gundberg (1986) trace the flawed and correct arguments. Searle (1971) gives general proofs of the independence and Cochran theorems in the style most linear-models texts follow. For nonnegative definite \A and \B, the condition  Sigma\A Sigma\B Sigma= m0 of Christensen (2020, Theorem 1.3.8) is in fact equivalent to \A Sigma\B= m0 (@exr-qf-singular-independence), so that theorem adds nothing to @thm-qf-indep-quadratic even for singular  Sigma, whereas his Theorem 1.3.9, for general symmetric \A and \B, does. That the independence of  ar{Y} and S^2 characterizes the normal distribution was shown by Lukacs (1942). References - Christensen, Ronald (2020). Plane Answers to Complex Questions: The Theory of Linear Models. 5th edition. Cham: Springer. - Cochran, William G. (1934). The Distribution of Quadratic Forms in a Normal System, with Applications to the Analysis of Covariance. Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society 30(2), 178–191. - Craig, Allen T. (1943). Note on the Independence of Certain Quadratic Forms. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 14(2), 195–197. - Driscoll, Michael F. and Gundberg, William R. (1986). A History of the Development of Craig’s Theorem. The American Statistician 40(1), 65–70. - Fisher, Ronald A. (1928). The General Sampling Distribution of the Multiple Correlation Coefficient. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A 121(788), 654–673. - Ghosh, B. K. (1973). Some Monotonicity Theorems for \chi^2, F and t Distributions with Applications. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B 35(3), 480–492. - Gil-Pelaez, J. (1951). Note on the Inversion Theorem. Biometrika 38(3/4), 481–482. - Imhof, J. P. (1961). Computing the Distribution of Quadratic Forms in Normal Variables. Biometrika 48(3/4), 419–426. - Johnson, Norman L., Kotz, Samuel and Balakrishnan, N. (1995). Continuous Univariate Distributions. 2nd edition. New York: Wiley. - Lukacs, Eugene (1942). A Characterization of the Normal Distribution. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 13(1), 91–93. - Mathai, A. M. and Provost, Serge B. (1992). Quadratic Forms in Random Variables: Theory and Applications. New York: Marcel Dekker. - Patnaik, P. B. (1949). The Non-Central \chi^2- and F-Distributions and Their Applications. Biometrika 36(1/2), 202–232. - Rencher, Alvin C. and Schaalje, G. Bruce (2008). Linear Models in Statistics. 2nd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - Satterthwaite, Franklin E. (1946). An Approximate Distribution of Estimates of Variance Components. Biometrics Bulletin 2(6), 110–114. - Searle, Shayle R. (1971). Linear Models. New York: Wiley. - Seber, George A. F. and Lee, Alan J. (2003). Linear Regression Analysis. 2nd edition. Hoboken, NJ: Wiley. - von Neumann, John (1941). Distribution of the Ratio of the Mean Square Successive Difference to the Variance. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 12(4), 367–395.

title: Projections: The Geometry of Least Squares
content: Projections: The Geometry of Least Squares Least squares chooses the point of a subspace that is closest to the data. Everything else in this chapter follows from that one statement: the normal equations, why fitted values are unique when coefficients are not, the orthogonal decompositions behind every sum of squares, the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, R^2 as a squared cosine, leverage, generalized least squares, and how the projection should actually be computed. What you need. Chapter 1 (rank, inverses, eigenvalues), Chapter 5 (the linear model and least squares). Random vectors (Chapter 2) appear only in a few remarks. Roadmap - Least squares as a nearest-point problem - The subspaces we need - Orthogonal projection - Least squares via projection - Nested models and sequential projection - The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem - Reparameterization, centring and R² - Leverage as geometry - Other inner products - Computation - Projection in the population: best linear prediction - Summary and notes

title: 6.1 Least squares as a nearest-point problem
content:
Least squares as a nearest-point problem Chapter 5 introduced least squares as a calculus problem: write down the sum of squared errors as a function of the coefficients, differentiate, set the derivative to zero. That route gets the right answer, but it hides the structure of the answer. It treats the coefficient vector  beta as the basic unknown. It needs \X\T\X to be invertible before it can say anything. And it gives no hint of why some quantities, such as fitted values, residuals and sums of squares, behave well in every model, while others, such as individual coefficients, can be fragile or not defined at all. This chapter starts from a different place. Instead of the p-dimensional space where  beta lives, it works in the n-dimensional space where the data live. Two pictures of the same data A regression data set with n observations and a single regressor is usually drawn as a scatterplot: n points in the plane, one for each observation, with the regressor on one axis and the response on the other. Call this the variable space picture. It is the right picture for seeing the shape of a relationship, but it scales badly. With k regressors it needs k+1 dimensions, and it has no natural place for the model’s coefficients. The other picture turns this around. Stack the n responses into a single vector \y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)\T, and regard it as one point in \Real^n. Each column of the model matrix \X is also a vector in \Real^n: the intercept column is  one, and the column for a regressor holds its n observed values. This is the observation space picture. Its dimension is the sample size, which is usually far more than three. But it contains only p+1 vectors of interest, and those always span a subspace of dimension at most p+1. Most of the geometry happens in a subspace small enough to draw. In observation space, the linear model \E(\Y) = \X beta, \qquad  beta\in\Real^p, says one thing: the mean vector \E(\Y) lies in the set \C(\X) = \{\X b :  b\in\Real^p\}, the column space of \X. That set is a subspace of \Real^n. The coefficients  beta are the coordinates of \E(\Y) with respect to the columns of \X, but the claim itself is only about where \E(\Y) is. It does not depend on which spanning vectors are used to describe the subspace. The least squares principle, restated The observed \y is almost never in \C(\X), because noise moves it off the subspace. A natural estimate of \E(\Y) is the point of \C(\X) that is closest to \y. With Euclidean distance, this is exactly least squares: 
orm{\y-\X b}^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n  igl(y_i-\x_{(i)}\T b igr)^2, where \x_{(i)}\T is the ith row of \X. Minimizing over  b is the same as searching \C(\X) for the point nearest to \y. [Least squares] A vector \hbeta\in\Real^p is a least squares estimate of  beta if 
orm{\y-\X\hbeta} \le 
orm{\y-\X b} \qquad	ext{for every }  b\in\Real^p. The vector \hY=\X\hbeta is the fitted value vector, and \he=\y-\hY is the residual vector. The definition does not assume that the minimizer is unique, and deliberately so. In Section 6.4 we will see that the nearest point \hY is always unique. The coefficient vector \hbeta that produces it is unique only when the columns of \X are linearly independent. A picture with three observations The smallest case that still shows all the geometry has n=3 and p=2. Then \C(\X) is a plane through the origin in \Real^3, and \y is a point somewhere off the plane. [Three observations] Take responses \y=(1,4,2)\T at regressor values \x=(0,1,3)\T, with an intercept, so that \X=[ one,\x]. The least squares fit (computed by the listing below) is \hY = (2.143,\ 2.286,\ 2.571)\T,\qquad \he = (-1.143,\ 1.714,\ -0.571)\T, with intercept 2.143 and slope 0.143. Two facts stand out. First, the residual is orthogonal to both columns of \X: the entries of \he sum to zero, and \x\T\he = 0. Second, the squared lengths add: 
orm{\y}^2=21.000 = 16.429 + 4.571 = 
orm{\hY}^2+
orm{\he}^2 . Figure 6.1.1 shows the configuration. The fitted vector is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from \y to the plane. [Figure 6.1.1. Least squares with n=3 observations. The model’s column space \C(\X) is the plane spanned by  one and \x. The fitted vector \hY=\M\y is the point of the plane nearest to \y, and the residual \he=\y-\hY is perpendicular to the plane.] Figure 6.1.1. Least squares with n=3 observations. The model’s column space \C(\X) is the plane spanned by  one and \x. The fitted vector \hY=\M\y is the point of the plane nearest to \y, and the residual \he=\y-\hY is perpendicular to the plane. [Least squares with n=3 observations. The model’s column space \C(\X) is the plane spanned by  one and \x. The fitted vector \hY=\M\y is the point of the plane nearest to \y, and the residual \he=\y-\hY is perpendicular to the plane.] Least squares with n=3 observations. The model’s column space \C(\X) is the plane spanned by  one and \x. The fitted vector \hY=\M\y is the point of the plane nearest to \y, and the residual \he=\y-\hY is perpendicular to the plane. import numpy as np y = np.array([1.0, 4.0, 2.0]) X = np.column_stack([np.ones(3), [0.0, 1.0, 3.0]]) # intercept and one regressor beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None) y_hat = X @ beta_hat # the point of C(X) nearest to y e_hat = y - y_hat # the residual vector print("fitted ", y_hat) print("residual", e_hat) print("X^T e ", X.T @ e_hat) # zero: the residual is orthogonal to C(X) The two facts in @exm-proj-three-points are not coincidences of this data set. They are the whole theory in miniature. The residual is orthogonal to the subspace because \hY is the nearest point, and the squared lengths add because the two pieces are orthogonal. The rest of the chapter makes these two statements precise and follows their consequences. Fitted values are determined by the subspace \C(\X). Coefficients are determined by the basis used to describe it. Anything that depends only on \C(\X) is unchanged by reparameterization, by rescaling or recoding regressors, and by rank deficiency. This covers fitted values, residuals, sums of squares, R^2 and leverages. Plan of the chapter Section 6.2 collects the facts about subspaces that the geometry needs. Section 6.3 proves that nearest points exist and are unique, and identifies the matrices that compute them: the symmetric idempotent matrices, including \X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T for every generalized inverse. Section 6.4 applies this to least squares. Section 6.5 studies nested subspaces, which is where sums of squares come from. Section 6.6 proves the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, which says what a single coefficient in a multiple regression measures. Section 6.7 covers reparameterization and R^2, and Section 6.8 covers leverage. Section 6.9 replaces the Euclidean inner product with a general one, the step that leads to generalized least squares. Section 6.10 shows how the projection should be computed in floating point.

title: 6.2 The subspaces we need
content:
The subspaces we need This section gathers the vector-space facts used in the rest of the chapter. Readers who have worked through Chapter 1 can skim the definitions. The results on orthogonal complements, especially @lem-proj-null-colspace and @thm-proj-direct-sum, are used constantly afterwards and are proved in full. Subspaces, spans and dimension A nonempty set \mathcal S\subseteq\Real^n is a subspace if it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication:  u, v\in\mathcal S and a,b\in\Real imply a u+b v\in\mathcal S. Every subspace contains  zero. The span of vectors  v_1,\dots, v_k is the set of all their linear combinations. It is the smallest subspace containing them. A set of vectors is linearly independent if the only linear combination equal to  zero is the one with all coefficients zero. A basis for \mathcal S is a linearly independent set that spans \mathcal S. All bases of \mathcal S have the same number of elements, the dimension \dim\mathcal S. For an n	imes p matrix \A there are two subspaces we use constantly:  egin{aligned} \C(\A) &= \{\A b: b\in\Real^p\}\subseteq\Real^n &&	ext{(column space)},\ \Null(\A) &= \{ b\in\Real^p:\A b= zero\}\subseteq\Real^p &&	ext{(null space)}.\end{aligned} The rank of \A is ank(\A)=\dim\C(\A). Two standard facts from Chapter 1: row rank equals column rank, so ank(\A)=ank(\A\T); and the rank–nullity theorem ank(\A)+\dim\Null(\A)=p . {#eq-proj-rank-nullity} In regression, \C(\X) is the model space. \Null(\X) is the set of directions in which  beta can move without changing \X beta. It is \{ zero\} exactly when \X has full column rank. [A rank-deficient layout] Suppose n observations fall into g groups and \X=[ one,\, z_1,\dots, z_g], where  z_k is the indicator of group k. Since  z_1+\dots+ z_g= one, the vector (1,-1,\dots,-1)\T lies in \Null(\X). The g indicators are linearly independent (their supports are disjoint), so ank(\X)=g while p=g+1. By @eq-proj-rank-nullity, \Null(\X) is exactly the line spanned by (1,-1,\dots,-1)\T. The model space \C(\X)=\C([ z_1,\dots, z_g]) is the set of vectors that are constant within groups. Inner products, orthogonality and complements Unless stated otherwise \Real^n carries the Euclidean inner product \inner{ u}{ v}= u\T v and norm 
orm{ u}=( u\T u)^{1/2}. Vectors are orthogonal, written  u\perp v, if  u\T v=0. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \lvert u\T vvert\le
orm{ u}
orm{ v}, with equality iff one vector is a multiple of the other, lets us define the angle 	heta\in[0,\pi] between nonzero vectors by \cos	heta= rac{ u\T v}{
orm{ u}\,
orm{ v}} . {#eq-proj-cosine} The angle comes back in Section 6.7, where R^2 turns out to be a squared cosine. The Pythagorean identity  u\perp v \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
orm{ u+ v}^2=
orm{ u}^2+
orm{ v}^2 {#eq-proj-pythagoras} follows by expanding ( u+ v)\T( u+ v). The cross terms are the ones that vanish. [Orthogonal complement] The orthogonal complement of a subspace \mathcal S\subseteq\Real^n is \mathcal S\perpc=\{ v\in\Real^n: v\T u=0	ext{ for all } u\in\mathcal S\}. It is immediate that \mathcal S\perpc is a subspace and that \mathcal S\cap\mathcal S\perpc=\{ zero\}: a vector orthogonal to itself has zero length. To test whether  v\in\mathcal S\perpc it is enough to check orthogonality to a spanning set of \mathcal S. In particular,  v\in\C(\A)\perpc iff \A\T v= zero. For any n	imes p matrix \A, \Null(\A\T)=\C(\A)\perpc \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \Null(\A)=\C(\A\T)\perpc .  v\in\Null(\A\T) means \A\T v= zero, that is,  v is orthogonal to every column of \A, which is the same as  v\perp\C(\A). The second identity is the first applied to \A\T. Orthonormal bases and Gram–Schmidt Vectors  u_1,\dots, u_k are orthonormal if  u_i\T u_j is 1 for i=j and 0 otherwise. Orthonormal vectors are linearly independent: taking the inner product of \sum_j a_j u_j= zero with  u_i gives a_i=0. The coordinates of a vector  v\in\spn( u_1,\dots, u_k) are simply the inner products a_i= u_i\T v, with no linear system to solve. This is why orthonormal bases are so convenient. [Gram–Schmidt] Let  v_1,\dots, v_k be linearly independent. Define recursively  w_j= v_j-\sum_{i<j}( u_i\T v_j)\, u_i,\qquad  u_j= w_j/
orm{ w_j},\qquad j=1,\dots,k. Then each  w_j
eq zero. The vectors  u_1,\dots, u_k are orthonormal, and \spn( u_1,\dots, u_j)=\spn( v_1,\dots, v_j) for every j. Induction on j. Suppose the claims hold for j-1. The vector  w_j is  v_j minus an element of \spn( u_1,\dots, u_{j-1})=\spn( v_1,\dots, v_{j-1}). If  w_j were zero,  v_j would lie in that span, contradicting independence. For l<j,  u_l\T w_j= u_l\T v_j-\sum_{i<j}( u_i\T v_j)\, u_l\T u_i = u_l\T v_j- u_l\T v_j=0, so  u_j is orthogonal to its predecessors. Finally,  u_j\in\spn( u_1,\dots, u_{j-1}, v_j)=\spn( v_1,\dots, v_j) and  v_j\in\spn( u_1,\dots, u_j), so the two spans agree. Two consequences are used repeatedly. Every subspace has an orthonormal basis (apply Gram–Schmidt to any basis). And any orthonormal basis of a subspace \mathcal S can be extended to an orthonormal basis of \Real^n: extend it to a basis of \Real^n in any way, then apply Gram–Schmidt, which leaves the first vectors unchanged. Section 6.10 shows that Gram–Schmidt, written in matrix form, is the QR factorization. Direct sums and the orthogonal decomposition For subspaces \mathcal S,\mathcal T, the sum \mathcal S+\mathcal T=\{ u+ v: u\in\mathcal S, v\in\mathcal T\} is a subspace. When \mathcal S\cap\mathcal T=\{ zero\} the sum is direct, written \mathcal S\dirsum\mathcal T. Every element then decomposes as  u+ v in exactly one way: if  u+ v= u'+ v' then  u- u'= v'- v lies in both subspaces and so is zero. When in addition \mathcal S\perp\mathcal T, the sum is an orthogonal direct sum. [Orthogonal decomposition] For every subspace \mathcal S\subseteq\Real^n, \Real^n=\mathcal S\dirsum\mathcal S\perpc, \qquad \dim\mathcal S+\dim\mathcal S\perpc=n, \qquad (\mathcal S\perpc)\perpc=\mathcal S . Hence every \y\in\Real^n can be written uniquely as \y= u+ v with  u\in\mathcal S and  v\perp\mathcal S. Let  u_1,\dots, u_r be an orthonormal basis of \mathcal S, extended to an orthonormal basis  u_1,\dots, u_n of \Real^n. A vector \y=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i u_i is orthogonal to \mathcal S iff a_1=\dots=a_r=0, so \mathcal S\perpc=\spn( u_{r+1},\dots, u_n) has dimension n-r. Writing \y=\sum_{i\le r}a_i u_i+\sum_{i>r}a_i u_i exhibits the decomposition, and it is unique because \mathcal S\cap\mathcal S\perpc=\{ zero\}. By the same argument with the roles of the two index sets swapped, (\mathcal S\perpc)\perpc=\spn( u_1,\dots, u_r)=\mathcal S. Combining @thm-proj-direct-sum with @lem-proj-null-colspace gives a matrix fact used in almost every later chapter. For any n	imes p matrix \A: 1. \Null(\A\T\A)=\Null(\A); 2. \C(\A\T\A)=\C(\A\T) and \C(\A\A\T)=\C(\A); 3. ank(\A\T\A)=ank(\A\A\T)=ank(\A); 4. \C(\A)\perpc=\Null(\A\T) and \Real^p=\C(\A\T)\dirsum\Null(\A). (a) If \A b= zero then \A\T\A b= zero. Conversely, \A\T\A b= zero gives  b\T\A\T\A b=
orm{\A b}^2=0, so \A b= zero. (b) By @lem-proj-null-colspace applied to the symmetric matrix \A\T\A, and then (a) and @lem-proj-null-colspace again, \C(\A\T\A)=\Null(\A\T\A)\perpc=\Null(\A)\perpc=(\C(\A\T)\perpc)\perpc=\C(\A\T), using (\mathcal S\perpc)\perpc=\mathcal S in the last step. The second identity is the first applied to \A\T. (c) Take dimensions in (b) and use ank(\A\T)=ank(\A). (d) This is @lem-proj-null-colspace and @thm-proj-direct-sum. Part (b) is the reason the normal equations \X\T\X b=\X\T\y can always be solved: the right-hand side lies in \C(\X\T)=\C(\X\T\X). We come back to this in Section 6.4. For subspaces \mathcal S_1,\mathcal S_2\subseteq\Real^n, (\mathcal S_1+\mathcal S_2)\perpc=\mathcal S_1\perpc\cap\mathcal S_2\perpc \qquad	ext{and}\qquad (\mathcal S_1\cap\mathcal S_2)\perpc=\mathcal S_1\perpc+\mathcal S_2\perpc . A vector is orthogonal to \mathcal S_1+\mathcal S_2 iff it is orthogonal to every  u_1+ u_2, which (taking  u_2= zero or  u_1= zero) is the case iff it is orthogonal to both subspaces. For the second identity, apply the first to \mathcal S_1\perpc and \mathcal S_2\perpc: (\mathcal S_1\perpc+\mathcal S_2\perpc)\perpc=\mathcal S_1\cap\mathcal S_2, and take complements of both sides. @lem-proj-complement-intersection is what we need to describe reduced models defined by linear constraints (@thm-proj-constraint-space). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Show that \mathcal S\perpc is a subspace for any set \mathcal S (not necessarily a subspace), and that \mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal T implies \mathcal T\perpc\subseteq\mathcal S\perpc. Show that \mathcal S\perpc=\spn(\mathcal S)\perpc. B. Practice [B1] A one-way layout has three groups of sizes 2,2,1 and model matrix \X=[ one, z_1, z_2, z_3]. Find bases for \C(\X), \Null(\X), \C(\X\T) and \C(\X)\perpc, and check that the dimensions agree with @eq-proj-rank-nullity and @thm-proj-direct-sum. [B2] Show that \C(\A\B)\subseteq\C(\A), and deduce ank(\A\B)\le\min\{ank(\A),ank(\B)\}. Show that \C(\A\B)=\C(\A) whenever \B has full row rank. C. Going deeper [C1] For subspaces \mathcal S,\mathcal T\subseteq\Real^n, prove \dim(\mathcal S+\mathcal T)=\dim\mathcal S+\dim\mathcal T-\dim(\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T). Use it to show that two r-dimensional subspaces of \Real^n with 2r>n must share a nonzero vector.

title: 6.3 Orthogonal projection
content:
Orthogonal projection Nearest points [Projection theorem] Let \mathcal S be a subspace of \Real^n and \y\in\Real^n. There is exactly one \hat{\y}\in\mathcal S such that 
orm{\y-\hat{\y}}\le
orm{\y- u}\qquad	ext{for all } u\in\mathcal S . It is the unique \hat{\y}\in\mathcal S with \y-\hat{\y}\perp\mathcal S. Moreover, for every  u\in\mathcal S, 
orm{\y- u}^2=
orm{\y-\hat{\y}}^2+
orm{\hat{\y}- u}^2 . {#eq-proj-distance-split} By @thm-proj-direct-sum there is a unique decomposition \y=\hat{\y}+ v with \hat{\y}\in\mathcal S and  v\in\mathcal S\perpc. For  u\in\mathcal S, \y- u= v+(\hat{\y}- u), where  v\perp\mathcal S and \hat{\y}- u\in\mathcal S. The Pythagorean identity @eq-proj-pythagoras then gives @eq-proj-distance-split. The right-hand side is at least 
orm{\y-\hat{\y}}^2, with equality iff  u=\hat{\y}. So \hat{\y} is the unique nearest point. If some other  w\in\mathcal S also had \y- w\perp\mathcal S, then \y= w+(\y- w) would be a second decomposition, contradicting uniqueness. The theorem has two halves, and it helps to keep them apart. The variational half says \hat{\y} minimizes a distance. The orthogonality half says the error \y-\hat{\y} is perpendicular to the subspace. The first half explains why least squares is a sensible estimation principle. The second is what we compute with, because orthogonality is a set of linear equations. The projection as a matrix Write  P_{\mathcal S}\y for the nearest point \hat{\y}. The map \y\mapsto P_{\mathcal S}\y is linear: if \y_k=\hat{\y}_k+ v_k are the decompositions of \y_1 and \y_2, then a\y_1+b\y_2=(a\hat{\y}_1+b\hat{\y}_2)+(a v_1+b v_2) is a decomposition of the same kind, and by uniqueness it is the decomposition. A linear map on \Real^n is given by a unique n	imes n matrix, since two matrices that agree on every vector agree on the standard basis vectors and are therefore equal. [Orthogonal projection matrix] The orthogonal projection onto a subspace \mathcal S is the unique n	imes n matrix  P_{\mathcal S} such that, for every \y,  P_{\mathcal S}\y\in\mathcal S and \y- P_{\mathcal S}\y\perp\mathcal S. When \mathcal S=\C(\X) for the model matrix of a linear model, we write \M= P_{\C(\X)}. The most useful formula for  P_{\mathcal S} uses an orthonormal basis. Let the columns of the n	imes r matrix \Q be an orthonormal basis for \mathcal S, so that \Q\T\Q=\I_r. Then  P_{\mathcal S}=\Q\Q\T=\sum_{i=1}^r u_i u_i\T, where  u_1,\dots, u_r are the columns of \Q. For any \y, \Q\Q\T\y=\Q(\Q\T\y)\in\C(\Q)=\mathcal S, and \Q\T(\y-\Q\Q\T\y)=\Q\T\y-\Q\T\y= zero, so the difference is orthogonal to every column of \Q and hence to \mathcal S. By uniqueness, \Q\Q\T= P_{\mathcal S}. [Projections onto a line] For \mathcal S=\spn( v) with  v
e zero, the single vector  v/
orm{ v} is an orthonormal basis, so  P_{\mathcal S}= rac{ v v\T}{ v\T v}, \qquad  P_{\mathcal S}\y= rac{ v\T\y}{ v\T v}\, v . With  v= one this gives  P=n^{-1} one one\T, the matrix with every entry 1/n, and  P\y= ar y\, one. The sample mean is a projection: fitting the intercept-only model replaces every observation by  ar y, and the residuals y_i- ar y form a vector in  one\perpc, the set of vectors whose entries sum to zero. Characterizing projection matrices Which matrices are orthogonal projections? @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula shows that every projection has the form \Q\Q\T, so it is symmetric, and \Q\Q\T\Q\Q\T=\Q\I\Q\T=\Q\Q\T, so it is idempotent. The converse is the basic recognition theorem. An n	imes n matrix  P is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace iff  P\T= P and  P^2= P. In that case the subspace is \C( P), and \I- P is the orthogonal projection onto \C( P)\perpc. Necessity was shown above. For sufficiency, let  P be symmetric and idempotent and let \y\in\Real^n. Certainly  P\y\in\C( P). For any  u= P b\in\C( P),  u\T(\y- P\y)= b\T P\T(\I- P)\y= b\T( P- P^2)\y=0, so \y- P\y\perp\C( P) and  P= P_{\C( P)}. For the last claim, \I- P is symmetric and idempotent, since (\I- P)^2=\I-2 P+ P^2=\I- P. It sends \y to \y- P\y\in\C( P)\perpc, and \y-(\I- P)\y= P\y\perp\C( P)\perpc. Before this theorem, checking that a matrix computes a projection meant thinking about subspaces. Afterwards it is two matrix identities. Also, a projection is determined by its range: if  P_1, P_2 are symmetric idempotent with \C( P_1)=\C( P_2), then  P_1= P_2, because both are the projection onto the same subspace. [Spectrum, rank and trace] Let  P be the orthogonal projection onto an r-dimensional subspace \mathcal S. Then: 1. every eigenvalue of  P is 0 or 1, and 1 has multiplicity r; 2. ank( P)=	r( P)=r; 3.  P v= v iff  v\in\mathcal S, and  P v= zero iff  v\in\mathcal S\perpc; 4.  v\T P v=
orm{ P v}^2\le
orm{ v}^2, so  P and \I- P are nonnegative definite. Write  P=\Q\Q\T as in @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula, and extend \Q to an orthogonal matrix \vect{U}=[\Q,\Q_\perp]. Then  P=\vect{U}\diag(\I_r, zero)\vect{U}\T is a spectral decomposition, which gives (a). Rank and trace of a symmetric matrix are the number of nonzero eigenvalues and their sum, which gives (b). Directly, 	r(\Q\Q\T)=	r(\Q\T\Q)=	r(\I_r)=r. Part (c) restates the projection theorem: the nearest point of \mathcal S to a vector already in \mathcal S is the vector itself, and  v\perp\mathcal S iff  zero is its nearest point. For (d),  v\T P v= v\T P\T P v, and 
orm{ v}^2=
orm{ P v}^2+
orm{(\I- P) v}^2 by Pythagoras. The identity ank=	r gets a lot of use. The dimension of a subspace, which is the “degrees of freedom” of every sum of squares in this book, can be read off as a sum of diagonal entries without finding a basis. Generalized inverses @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula needs an orthonormal basis. In statistics the subspace usually comes as the column space of a model matrix \X whose columns are not orthonormal and may not even be independent. To write \M directly in terms of \X we need a substitute for (\X\T\X)^{-1} that exists even when \X\T\X is singular. [Generalized inverse] A generalized inverse of an m	imes k matrix \A is any k	imes m matrix \A\ginv such that \A\A\ginv\A=\A. If \A is square and nonsingular, multiplying \A\A\ginv\A=\A on both sides by \A^{-1} gives \A\ginv=\A^{-1}, so the generalized inverse is unique and equal to the inverse. When \A is singular there are infinitely many. [Existence] Every matrix has a generalized inverse. If \A has rank r and is permuted so that \A= egin{pmatrix}\A_{11}&\A_{12}\\A_{21}&\A_{22}\end{pmatrix} with \A_{11} an r	imes r nonsingular block, then \A\ginv= egin{pmatrix}\A_{11}^{-1}& zero\ zero& zero\end{pmatrix} (permuted back) is a generalized inverse. A rank-r matrix has r independent rows and r independent columns, and the submatrix where they cross is nonsingular (Chapter 1). This guarantees the block form. Since the first r columns are a basis for the column space,  egin{pmatrix}\A_{12}\\A_{22}\end{pmatrix}= egin{pmatrix}\A_{11}\\A_{21}\end{pmatrix}\B for some \B, so \B=\A_{11}^{-1}\A_{12} and \A_{22}=\A_{21}\A_{11}^{-1}\A_{12}. Multiplying out, \A\A\ginv\A= egin{pmatrix}\I& zero\\A_{21}\A_{11}^{-1}& zero\end{pmatrix}\A = egin{pmatrix}\A_{11}&\A_{12}\\A_{21}&\A_{21}\A_{11}^{-1}\A_{12}\end{pmatrix}=\A . \qedhere Among the many generalized inverses, one is singled out by extra symmetry conditions. The Moore–Penrose inverse \A^{+} is the unique matrix satisfying \A\A^+\A=\A, \A^+\A\A^+=\A^+, and both \A\A^+ and \A^+\A symmetric (Penrose 1955). Section 6.10 computes it from the singular value decomposition. For projections we will need none of these extra conditions, and that is the point of the next result. Let \X be n	imes p and let \G be any generalized inverse of \X\T\X. Then: 1. \X\G\X\T\X=\X and \X\T\X\G\X\T=\X\T; 2. \X\G\X\T does not depend on the choice of generalized inverse; 3. \X\G\X\T is symmetric, even when \G is not. By @cor-proj-gram-colspace(b), \C(\X\T)=\C(\X\T\X), so there is a p	imes n matrix \B with \X\T=\X\T\X\B. Transposing, \X=\B\T\X\T\X. Then \X\G\X\T\X=\B\T(\X\T\X)\G(\X\T\X)=\B\T\X\T\X=\X, which is the first identity in (a). The second follows the same way, using \X\T=\X\T\X\B on the right. For (b) and (c), \X\G\X\T=\B\T(\X\T\X)\G(\X\T\X)\B=\B\T\X\T\X\B , which involves no \G at all, and (\B\T\X\T\X\B)\T=\B\T\X\T\X\B. For any n	imes p matrix \X and any generalized inverse (\X\T\X)\ginv, \M=\X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T is the orthogonal projection onto \C(\X). In particular ank(\M)=	r(\M)=ank(\X). If \X has full column rank, \M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T. By @lem-proj-ginverse-invariance, \M is symmetric and \M^2=\X(\X\T\X)\ginv igl[\X\T\X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T igr]=\X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T=\M. By @thm-proj-sym-idem, \M is the projection onto \C(\M). Clearly \C(\M)\subseteq\C(\X), and \M\X=\X (again by the lemma) shows \C(\X)\subseteq\C(\M). The rank statement is @prp-proj-trace-rank(b). It is worth pausing on how strong @thm-proj-M-formula is. The matrix (\X\T\X)\ginv can be almost anything: symmetric or not, reflexive or not, with entries of any size. The sandwich \X(\cdot)\X\T removes all of that freedom. We will see in Section 6.4 that this is exactly the difference between coefficients and fitted values, made concrete. [The one-way layout] In the setting of @exm-proj-oneway-rank, sort the observations by group and let group k have n_k members. The model space is spanned by the orthogonal vectors  z_1,\dots, z_g, so by @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula with  u_k= z_k/\sqrt{n_k}, \M=\sum_{k=1}^g rac{ z_k z_k\T}{n_k} = egin{pmatrix} n_1^{-1} one_{n_1} one_{n_1}\T & & \ & \ddots & \ & & n_g^{-1} one_{n_g} one_{n_g}\T \end{pmatrix}, a block-diagonal matrix of within-group averaging operators. \M\y replaces each observation by its group mean. The intercept column adds nothing to \C(\X), so it does not appear, and 	r(\M)=\sum_k n_k/n_k=g=ank(\X). We got here without a generalized inverse. @thm-proj-M-formula guarantees that any generalized inverse of the singular (g+1)	imes(g+1) matrix \X\T\X produces this same matrix. Section 6.4 checks this numerically. Sums and products of projections Complicated subspaces are often built from simpler ones, and their projections are built the same way. Let  P_1, P_2 be orthogonal projections. Then  P_1+ P_2 is an orthogonal projection iff  P_1 P_2= zero, that is, iff \C( P_1)\perp\C( P_2). In that case it projects onto \C( P_1)\dirsum\C( P_2).  P_1+ P_2 is always symmetric, and ( P_1+ P_2)^2= P_1+ P_2+ P_1 P_2+ P_2 P_1. So it is idempotent iff  P_1 P_2+ P_2 P_1= zero. If  P_1 P_2= zero, then transposing gives  P_2 P_1= zero and the condition holds. Conversely, suppose  P_1 P_2+ P_2 P_1= zero. Multiplying on the left by  P_1 gives  P_1 P_2+ P_1 P_2 P_1= zero, and on the right by  P_1 gives  P_1 P_2 P_1+ P_2 P_1= zero. Subtracting,  P_1 P_2= P_2 P_1, and then 2 P_1 P_2= zero. The equivalence with orthogonality of ranges holds because  P_1 P_2= zero says exactly that every vector of \C( P_2) is sent to  zero by  P_1, that is (@prp-proj-trace-rank(c)), lies in \C( P_1)\perpc. Finally, \C( P_1+ P_2)\subseteq\C( P_1)+\C( P_2), and for  u= P_1 u+ P_2 u in that sum we have ( P_1+ P_2) u= u, so the ranges agree. By induction, if  P_1,\dots, P_k are projections with  P_i P_j= zero for i
e j, their sum projects onto the orthogonal direct sum of their ranges. When the sum is \I, we get an orthogonal decomposition \y= P_1\y+\dots+ P_k\y,\qquad 
orm{\y}^2=
orm{ P_1\y}^2+\dots+
orm{ P_k\y}^2 . Every analysis of variance table in this book is a table of such a decomposition. Products behave differently.  P_1 P_2 need not be symmetric or idempotent, and it is generally not a projection. @exr-proj-product shows that it is one iff  P_1 and  P_2 commute, in which case it projects onto \C( P_1)\cap\C( P_2). The most important instance is the nested case \C( P_2)\subseteq\C( P_1), treated in Section 6.5. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Let \mathcal S=\spn\{(1,1,0)\T,(0,1,1)\T\}. Compute  P_{\mathcal S} in two ways: by Gram–Schmidt and @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula, and by @thm-proj-M-formula. Verify symmetry, idempotence and 	r P_{\mathcal S}=2. Find \mathcal S\perpc and check that \I- P_{\mathcal S} projects onto it. [A2] Show that a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues all lie in \{0,1\} is an orthogonal projection. Give a non-symmetric 2	imes2 matrix with eigenvalues 0 and 1 that is not idempotent, and one that is idempotent. [A3] Let  P be an orthogonal projection and a,b real numbers. Show that the eigenvalues of a P+b\I are b and a+b. Show that when b
e0 and a+b
e0, (a P+b\I)^{-1}= rac1b\Bigl(\I- rac{a}{a+b} P\Bigr). Use this to invert the equicorrelation matrix (1-ho)\I+ho one one\T. [A4] Show that if \G is a generalized inverse of the symmetric matrix \X\T\X, then so is \G\T, and so is \G\X\T\X\G\T. Which of the four Penrose conditions does the last one satisfy? B. Practice [B1] Let  P_1, P_2 be orthogonal projections. Show that  P_1 P_2 is an orthogonal projection iff  P_1 P_2= P_2 P_1, and that in this case it projects onto \C( P_1)\cap\C( P_2). Hint: for the range, show  P_1 P_2 u= u iff  u lies in both subspaces. If  P_1 P_2= P_2 P_1, then ( P_1 P_2)\T= P_2 P_1= P_1 P_2, and ( P_1 P_2)^2= P_1 P_2 P_2 P_1= P_1 P_2 P_1= P_1 P_1 P_2= P_1 P_2. So the product is symmetric and idempotent. Conversely, if  P_1 P_2 is an orthogonal projection, it is symmetric, so  P_1 P_2=( P_1 P_2)\T= P_2 P_1. For the range: if  u lies in both subspaces, then  P_1 P_2 u= P_1 u= u. If  P_1 P_2 u= u, then  u\in\C( P_1), and also  u= P_2 P_1 u\in\C( P_2). A projection’s range is the set of vectors it fixes, so \C( P_1 P_2)=\C( P_1)\cap\C( P_2). [B2] Let \G_0 be a generalized inverse of \A. 1. Show that \G_0+(\I-\G_0\A) U+\V(\I-\A\G_0) is a generalized inverse of \A for all conformable  U,\V. 2. Show that every generalized inverse \G of \A has this form. Hint: take  U=\G-\G_0 and \V=\G_0\A(\G-\G_0), and use \A(\G-\G_0)\A= zero. 3. Conclude that a matrix has a unique generalized inverse iff it is square and nonsingular. Parts a,b. For (a), multiply out: \A igl[\G_0+(\I-\G_0\A) U+\V(\I-\A\G_0) igr]\A =\A\G_0\A+(\A-\A\G_0\A) U\A+\A\V(\A-\A\G_0\A)=\A. For (b), put  m\Delta=\G-\G_0, so that \A m\Delta\A=\A-\A= zero. With  U= m\Delta and \V=\G_0\A m\Delta, (\I-\G_0\A) m\Delta+\G_0\A m\Delta(\I-\A\G_0) = m\Delta-\G_0\A m\Delta+\G_0\A m\Delta-\G_0(\A m\Delta\A)\G_0= m\Delta , so the formula reproduces \G_0+ m\Delta=\G. [B3] Using the singular value decomposition, show that (\X\T\X)^+\X\T=\X^+ and \X\X^+=\M. Show also that \X^+=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T when \X has full column rank. C. Going deeper [C1] Show that \M is the only n	imes n matrix  P satisfying  P\X=\X,  P\T= P and ank( P)=ank(\X). Is the rank condition necessary? Is symmetry?

title: 6.4 Least squares via projection
content: Least squares via projection We now return to the linear model \Y=\X beta+ e, with \X an n imes p matrix of rank r\le p, and \M the orthogonal projection onto \C(\X). Nothing in this section uses probability. The results hold for every data vector \y and so apply whatever the distribution of the errors. The characterization of least squares estimates [Least squares is projection] A vector \hbeta is a least squares estimate of beta iff \X\hbeta=\M\y . Consequently the fitted values \hY=\M\y and residuals \he=(\I-\M)\y are the same for every least squares estimate. Apply the projection theorem (@thm-proj-projection-theorem) with \mathcal S=\C(\X) and u=\X b. By @eq-proj-distance-split, orm{\y-\X b}^2= orm{\y-\M\y}^2+ orm{\M\y-\X b}^2 \qquad ext{for every } b\in\Real^p . The first term does not involve b, and the second is zero iff \X b=\M\y. Such a b exists because \M\y\in\C(\X). The orthogonality half of the projection theorem turns this into linear equations. The residual \y-\X b is orthogonal to \C(\X) iff it is orthogonal to every column of \X, that is, iff \X\T(\y-\X b)= zero. [Normal equations] The normal equations \X\T\X b=\X\T\y {#eq-proj-normal-equations} are consistent for every \y, and their solutions are exactly the least squares estimates. One solution is \hbeta=(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T\y, for any generalized inverse, and the set of all solutions is \hbeta+\Null(\X)=\{\hbeta+ v:\X v= zero\}. In particular, the least squares estimate is unique iff ank(\X)=p, and then \hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\y. A vector b solves @eq-proj-normal-equations iff \y-\X b\perp\C(\X). Since \X b\in\C(\X) automatically, this holds iff \y=\X b+(\y-\X b) is the orthogonal decomposition of \y, that is, iff \X b=\M\y. By @thm-proj-ls-projection this is the same as b being a least squares estimate. For the particular solution, \X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T\y=\M\y by @thm-proj-M-formula. Finally, \X b=\M\y=\X\hbeta iff \X( b-\hbeta)= zero, and \Null(\X)=\{ zero\} iff ank(\X)=p by @eq-proj-rank-nullity. The logic of this proof runs opposite to the usual calculus derivation, and the difference matters. Setting a gradient to zero finds stationary points. One then has to argue separately that they are minima and that one exists. Here existence, minimality and the full solution set all come from the decomposition \Real^n=\C(\X)\dirsum\C(\X)\perpc. The consistency of the normal equations, which can look surprising when \X\T\X is singular, is just the statement \X\T\y\in\C(\X\T)=\C(\X\T\X) from @cor-proj-gram-colspace. Fitted values and residuals Collecting the consequences for \hY=\M\y and \he=(\I-\M)\y: For any data vector \y: 1. \X\T\he= zero and \hY\T\he=0; 2. if one\in\C(\X) (for example, the model has an intercept), then \sum_i\hat{\varepsilon}_i=0 and the mean of the fitted values is ar y; 3. orm{\y}^2= orm{\hY}^2+ orm{\he}^2; 4. orm{\he}^2=\y\T(\I-\M)\y and orm{\hY}^2=\y\T\M\y; 5. if \y=\X beta+ e for some beta, then \hY=\X beta+\M e and \he=(\I-\M) e. (a) is the orthogonality of \he to \C(\X), and \hY\in\C(\X). For (b), one\in\C(\X) gives one\T\he=0, and then one\T\hY= one\T\y. (c) is Pythagoras. (d) uses symmetry and idempotence: orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2=\y\T(\I-\M)\T(\I-\M)\y=\y\T(\I-\M)\y. For (e), \M\X=\X and (\I-\M)\X= zero. Part (e) is simple but important. The residual vector does not depend on beta at all. It is the projection of the unobservable error vector onto the (n-r)-dimensional space \C(\X)\perpc. Everything about \sigma^2 that the data can reveal must therefore come from (\I-\M) e. If \E( e)= zero and \Cov( e)=\sigma^2\I, the expectation of a quadratic form (Chapter 2) gives \E orm{\he}^2=\E igl[ e\T(\I-\M) e igr]=\sigma^2 r(\I-\M)=\sigma^2(n-r), using @prp-proj-trace-rank. So orm{\he}^2/(n-r) is unbiased for \sigma^2. The divisor is the dimension of the space in which the residuals live, not the number of observations and not n-p. Chapter 7 develops the sampling theory, and Chapter 9 develops the decomposition. Coefficients are not unique; fitted values are When ank(\X)

title: 6.5 Nested models and sequential projection
content:
Nested models and sequential projection Statistical questions about linear models are almost always comparisons. Does a regressor matter? Are several group means equal? Is a curve needed, or will a line do? Each comparison sets a full model against a reduced model whose mean space is a subspace of the full one. This section studies the geometry of such nested pairs. Chapter 9 and Chapter 11 build the analysis of variance and the F test on it. Two nested subspaces Let \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X), with ranks r_0\le r. Write \Mo and \M for the two projections. [Nested projections] If \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X), then: 1. \M\Mo=\Mo\M=\Mo; 2. \M-\Mo is the orthogonal projection onto \C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X), the orthogonal complement of \C(\X_0) within \C(\X); 3. ank(\M-\Mo)=r-r_0; 4. (\I-\Mo)-(\I-\M)=\M-\Mo, and \Mo(\M-\Mo)=(\M-\Mo)(\I-\M)= zero. (a) Every column of \Mo lies in \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X) and is left unchanged by \M, so \M\Mo=\Mo. Transposing gives \Mo\M=\Mo. (b) \M-\Mo is symmetric, and by (a) (\M-\Mo)^2=\M-\M\Mo-\Mo\M+\Mo=\M-\Mo. By @thm-proj-sym-idem it projects onto its column space. If  v\in\C(\X) and  v\perp\C(\X_0), then (\M-\Mo) v= v- zero= v, so  v\in\C(\M-\Mo). Conversely, a vector  v=(\M-\Mo) u lies in \C(\X) and satisfies \Mo v=(\Mo-\Mo) u= zero. (c) 	r(\M-\Mo)=r-r_0 and @prp-proj-trace-rank. (d) Direct multiplication using (a). The theorem gives a three-way orthogonal decomposition of \Real^n, \Real^n=\underbrace{\C(\X_0)}_{\dim r_0} \;\dirsum\; \underbrace{\C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X)}_{\dim r-r_0} \;\dirsum\; \underbrace{\C(\X)\perpc}_{\dim n-r}, and correspondingly \I=\Mo+(\M-\Mo)+(\I-\M), with the three terms mutually orthogonal projections. Applying the decomposition to \y and using Pythagoras, 
orm{\y}^2=
orm{\Mo\y}^2+
orm{(\M-\Mo)\y}^2+
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2 . {#eq-proj-three-way} The middle term has a second reading that is the key to model comparison. Since (\I-\Mo)=(\M-\Mo)+(\I-\M) is an orthogonal sum, 
orm{(\M-\Mo)\y}^2 =
orm{(\I-\Mo)\y}^2-
orm{(\I-\M)\y}^2 =	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE}. {#eq-proj-extra-ss} The drop in residual sum of squares from the reduced to the full model is the squared length of a projection onto an (r-r_0)-dimensional space. That is why it has r-r_0 degrees of freedom, and why it is independent of SSE under normality: the two lie in orthogonal subspaces (Chapter 4). It also shows that SSE can never increase when the model space grows, with equality iff \M\y=\Mo\y. Figure 6.5.1. Nested projections. The fitted vector of the reduced model, \Mo\y, is also the projection of \M\y onto \C(\X_0). The three coloured pieces \Mo\y, (\M-\Mo)\y and (\I-\M)\y are mutually orthogonal. The dashed segment is the reduced model’s residual, whose squared length is the sum of the squared lengths of the two segments meeting at \M\y. Part (a) also says \Mo\y=\Mo(\M\y). Fitting the reduced model to the data gives the same result as fitting it to the full model’s fitted values. Projection can be done in stages (Figure 6.5.1). [Intercept inside simple regression] Let \X_0= one and \X=[ one,\x] with \x not constant. Then \C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X) is spanned by the centred regressor \x- ar x one=(\I-n^{-1} one one\T)\x, which lies in \C(\X) and is orthogonal to  one. By @exm-proj-line, \M-\Mo= rac{(\x- ar x one)(\x- ar x one)\T}{S_{xx}}, \qquad S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i- ar x)^2, and so \M\y= ar y one+ rac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}(\x- ar x one), \qquad S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i- ar x)(y_i- ar y). Reading off coordinates, the slope is S_{xy}/S_{xx} and the intercept is  ar y- ar x\,S_{xy}/S_{xx}. These are the familiar formulas, obtained without solving any equations, and the decomposition @eq-proj-three-way becomes \sum_i y_i^2 = n ar y^2+ rac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}+	ext{SSE}. Chains of subspaces The argument extends to any chain \C(\X_1)\subseteq\C(\X_2)\subseteq\dots\subseteq\C(\X_k) with projections \M_1,\dots,\M_k. Setting \M_0= zero and \M_{k+1}=\I, the differences \M_j-\M_{j-1} for j=1,\dots,k+1 are mutually orthogonal projections summing to \I. The corresponding lengths 
orm{(\M_j-\M_{j-1})\y}^2=	ext{SSE}_{j-1}-	ext{SSE}_j are the sequential sums of squares of Chapter 9. Their values depend on the order in which the subspaces are nested. A regressor added early can take credit that it would not get if added last. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem of Section 6.6 describes what the regressor added last actually contributes. [Order matters] For the state data of @exm-proj-fwl-crime, enter the three regressors after the intercept in two different orders. The listing computes each squared length 
orm{(\M_j-\M_{j-1})\y}^2 directly from the projections. Order A Order B --------------- -------- --------------- -------- poverty 102.49 single-parent 162.84 single-parent 80.04 urban 3.59 urban 0.27 poverty 16.37 residual 101.96 residual 101.96 Entered first, poverty accounts for 102.49 of the corrected total sum of squares 284.76. Entered last, it accounts for only 16.37. The residual sum of squares, and the total explained by all three regressors together (182.80), do not depend on the order, because the final subspace does not. The individual pieces do depend on the order, because the intermediate subspaces differ. Poverty and single parenthood are correlated, so whichever enters first takes the variation they share. The piece for the last regressor is the only one with an order-free meaning. By @thm-proj-fwl, it is the squared length of the projection of \y onto the part of that regressor orthogonal to all the others. import numpy as np import statsmodels.api as sm data = sm.datasets.statecrime.load_pandas().data.drop(index="District of Columbia") y = data["murder"].to_numpy() cols = {"poverty": data["poverty"], "single": data["single"], "urban": data["urban"]} def projection(Z): Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(Z) return Q @ Q.T # fine for n = 50; never do this for large n def sequential_ss(y, columns): """Squared lengths ||(M_j - M_{j-1}) y||^2 as columns enter one at a time.""" n = len(y) Z = np.ones((n, 1)) M_prev = projection(Z) pieces = {"mean": y @ M_prev @ y} for name, x in columns: Z = np.column_stack([Z, x]) M = projection(Z) pieces[name] = y @ (M - M_prev) @ y M_prev = M pieces["residual"] = y @ (np.eye(n) - M_prev) @ y return pieces order_a = sequential_ss(y, [(k, cols[k]) for k in ["poverty", "single", "urban"]]) order_b = sequential_ss(y, [(k, cols[k]) for k in ["single", "urban", "poverty"]]) for name in ["poverty", "single", "urban", "residual"]: print(f"{name:9s} order A: {order_a[name]:8.2f} order B: {order_b[name]:8.2f}") Two factors and when the pieces are orthogonal A sum of projections is a projection exactly when the pieces are orthogonal (@thm-proj-sum). In designed experiments, orthogonality comes from balance, and when it fails, it fails in ways that later chapters have to face. [Additive two-factor model, one observation per cell] Let factor A have a levels and factor B have b levels, with one observation y_{ij} for each of the n=ab combinations. Let  P_A project onto vectors that depend only on the A level, so  P_A\y has entries  ar y_{i\cdot}, and define  P_B similarly. Let  P_0=n^{-1} one one\T. Both \C( P_A) and \C( P_B) contain  one, so  P_A P_0= P_B P_0= P_0 by @thm-proj-nested. The crucial computation is  P_A P_B. Averaging over j with i fixed a vector that depends only on j gives the overall average of that vector. So for every \y the entries of  P_A( P_B\y) are all equal to b^{-1}\sum_j ar y_{\cdot j}= ar y_{\cdot\cdot}. Therefore  P_A P_B= P_0, and so ( P_A- P_0)( P_B- P_0)= P_0- P_0- P_0+ P_0= zero. The two centred factor spaces are orthogonal. By @thm-proj-sum, the additive model space has projection  P_0+( P_A- P_0)+( P_B- P_0)= P_A+ P_B- P_0, and \I= P_0+( P_A- P_0)+( P_B- P_0)+(\I- P_A- P_B+ P_0) is an orthogonal decomposition with ranks 1, a-1, b-1 and (a-1)(b-1). The residual projection sends y_{ij} to y_{ij}- ar y_{i\cdot}- ar y_{\cdot j}+ ar y_{\cdot\cdot}. The key step used the fact that every A level appears with every B level equally often. If cells are missing or unequally replicated,  P_A P_B
eq P_0, the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and the sum of squares for A depends on whether B was fitted first. Chapter 17 is about that situation. Reduced models defined by constraints Reduced models often come as constraints on the parameters of the full model, for example  eta_2= eta_3 or  eta_4=0, rather than as a smaller model matrix. In mean space, a constraint  Lambda\T beta= zero on an estimable function  Lambda\T= m P\T\X restricts  mu=\X beta to the subspace \mathcal S_0=\C(\X)\cap\Null( m P\T)=\{ mu\in\C(\X): m P\T mu= zero\}. To test the constraint we need the piece of \C(\X) that \mathcal S_0 removes. Let \M project onto \C(\X) and let  m P be an n	imes q matrix. If \mathcal S_0=\C(\X)\cap\Null( m P\T), then \mathcal S_0\perpc\cap\C(\X)=\C(\M m P). Hence the projection onto \mathcal S_0 is \M- P_{\C(\M m P)}, and \dim\mathcal S_0=r-ank(\M m P). By @lem-proj-complement-intersection and @lem-proj-null-colspace, \mathcal S_0\perpc=\C(\X)\perpc+\Null( m P\T)\perpc=\C(\X)\perpc+\C( m P). If  v\in\mathcal S_0\perpc\cap\C(\X), write  v= w+ m P m a with  w\perp\C(\X). Applying \M gives  v=\M v=\M m P m a\in\C(\M m P). Conversely, \M m P m a lies in \C(\X) and equals  m P m a-(\I-\M) m P m a\in\C( m P)+\C(\X)\perpc=\mathcal S_0\perpc. The remaining claims follow from @thm-proj-nested with the roles \C(\X_0)=\mathcal S_0. The subspace \C(\M m P) is the test space of the hypothesis. Its dimension ank(\M m P) counts how many independent restrictions the constraint really places on the mean. It can be smaller than q if some rows of the constraint are redundant. Chapter 11 uses exactly this space for the numerator of the F statistic. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] Construct the projections  P_A,  P_B and  P_0 of @exm-proj-two-factor for a=3, b=2 and verify  P_A P_B= P_0 numerically. Delete one observation and recompute. Show that the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and find the largest entry of ( P_A- P_0)( P_B- P_0). B. Practice [B1] With \C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X), show that 	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE}=
orm{\hY-\hY_0}^2, the squared distance between the two fitted vectors. \hY-\hY_0=(\M-\Mo)\y, and 
orm{(\M-\Mo)\y}^2=	ext{SSE}_0-	ext{SSE} by @eq-proj-extra-ss. [B2] In the model \E(\Y)= eta_0 one+ eta_1\x_1+ eta_2\x_2+ eta_3\x_3 with full-rank \X, the hypothesis  eta_2= eta_3 defines a reduced model with model matrix \X_0=[ one,\x_1,\x_2+\x_3]. Show that the test space \C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X) is spanned by (\I-\Mo)\x_2, and that (\I-\Mo)\x_2=-(\I-\Mo)\x_3. Verify that this agrees with @thm-proj-constraint-space for a suitable  m P. The two model spaces differ in dimension by one, so the test space is a line. The vector (\I-\Mo)\x_2 lies in \C(\X) and is orthogonal to \C(\X_0). It is nonzero, because \x_2\in\C(\X_0) would make the columns of \X dependent. Since \x_2+\x_3\in\C(\X_0), (\I-\Mo)(\x_2+\x_3)= zero. For @thm-proj-constraint-space, write the constraint as  lambda\T beta=0 with  lambda=(0,0,1,-1)\T, and take  m P=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1} lambda, so that  m P\T\X= lambda\T. Then \M m P= m P. Each column of \X_0 is \X m k with  lambda\T m k=0, so  m P\perp\C(\X_0) and  m P spans the same line. C. Going deeper [C1] Extend @exm-proj-two-factor to m\ge2 observations in every cell and a model with interaction. Find five mutually orthogonal projections summing to \I, corresponding to the grand mean, factor A, factor B, the interaction, and within-cell error, and find their ranks. Describe the action of each on \y in terms of cell, row, column and grand means.

title: 6.6 The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem
content:
The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem A coefficient in a multiple regression is often described as the effect of its regressor “holding the other regressors fixed”. In observational data nobody held anything fixed, so the phrase needs a precise meaning. The Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) theorem supplies one. A coefficient in a multiple regression equals the slope of a simple regression in which the other regressors have been projected out of both the response and the regressor of interest. Statement and proof Partition the model matrix and coefficients as \X=[\X_1,\X_2],\qquad  beta= egin{pmatrix} beta_1\ beta_2\end{pmatrix}, with \X_1 of size n	imes p_1 and \X_2 of size n	imes p_2, and assume \X has full column rank. Let \M_2 project onto \C(\X_2), and write 	ilde{\X}_1=(\I-\M_2)\X_1,\qquad 	ilde{\y}=(\I-\M_2)\y for the parts of \X_1 and \y that \X_2 cannot explain linearly. Each column of 	ilde{\X}_1 is the residual vector from regressing the corresponding column of \X_1 on \X_2. [Orthogonalizing a partitioned model space] Under the assumptions above: 1. \C(\X)=\C(\X_2)\dirsum\C(	ilde{\X}_1), and the two summands are orthogonal; 2. 	ilde{\X}_1 has full column rank; 3. \M=\M_2+	ilde{\M}_1, where 	ilde{\M}_1=	ilde{\X}_1(	ilde{\X}_1\T	ilde{\X}_1)^{-1}	ilde{\X}_1\T.
