title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.2 Mean and variance of quadratic forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_2(\bzero,\I)\) and \(\A=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}\) . Compute \(\Var(\Y\T\A\Y)\) directly, and compare with \(2\tr(\A^2)\) and with \(2\tr(\A_s^2)\) , where \(\A_s=\tfrac12(\A+\A\T)\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.1 (Canonical form of a normal quadratic form)
page: 4.2 Mean and variance of quadratic forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) and let \(\A\) be symmetric. Write \(\bSigma=\bL\bL\T\) with \(\bL\) of size \(n\times k\) , and take a spectral decomposition \(\bL\T\A\bL=\Q\bLambda\Q\T\) with \(\bLambda=\diag(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)\) . Put \(\bb=\Q\T\bL\T\A\bmu\) . Then \[ \Y\T\A\Y\;\overset{d}{=}\;\bmu\T\A\bmu+\sum_{j=1}^k\bigl(\lambda_jW_j^2+2b_jW_j\bigr), \qquad \W\sim\Normal_k(\bzero,\I_k). \] {#eq-qf-canonical} For \(\lambda_j\ne0\) the \(j\) th term equals \(\lambda_j(W_j+b_j/\lambda_j)^2-b_j^2/\lambda_j\) . The nonzero \(\lambda_j\) are the nonzero eigenvalues of \(\A\bSigma\) .

title: Theorem 4.2.3 (Moments of normal quadratic forms)
page: 4.2 Mean and variance of quadratic forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) , let \(\A\) and \(\B\) be symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices, and let \(\bm K\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix. Then \(\E(\Y\T\A\Y)=\tr(\A\bSigma)+\bmu\T\A\bmu\) ; \(\Var(\Y\T\A\Y)=2\tr\{(\A\bSigma)^2\}+4\bmu\T\A\bSigma\A\bmu\) ; \(\Cov(\bm K\Y,\Y\T\A\Y)=2\bm K\bSigma\A\bmu\) ; \(\Cov(\Y\T\A\Y,\Y\T\B\Y)=2\tr(\A\bSigma\B\bSigma)+4\bmu\T\A\bSigma\B\bmu\) .

title: Corollary 4.3.3 (Mahalanobis forms)
page: 4.3 When a quadratic form is chi-squared
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) . If \(\bSigma\) is positive definite, \((\Y-\bmu)\T\bSigma^{-1}(\Y-\bmu)\sim\chi^2(n)\) and \(\Y\T\bSigma^{-1}\Y\sim\chi^2(n,\bmu\T\bSigma^{-1}\bmu)\) . If \(\G\) is a symmetric generalized inverse of \(\bSigma\) and \(\bmu\in\C(\bSigma)\) , then \(\Y\T\G\Y\sim\chi^2\bigl(\rank(\bSigma),\bmu\T\G\bmu\bigr)\) .

title: Example (Correlated observations about a common level)
page: 4.3 When a quadratic form is chi-squared
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) with \(\bSigma\) positive definite, and suppose we want to measure how far \(\Y\) is from a common level \(m\bone\) . The generalized least squares level is \(\hat{m}=\bone\T\bSigma^{-1}\Y/\bone\T\bSigma^{-1}\bone\) , and the natural discrepancy is \((\Y-\hat{m}\bone)\T\bSigma^{-1}(\Y-\hat{m}\bone)=\Y\T\A\Y\) with \[ \A=\bSigma^{-1}-\frac{\bSigma^{-1}\bone\bone\T\bSigma^{-1}}{\bone\T\bSigma^{-1}\bone}. \] A direct multiplication gives \(\A\bSigma\A=\A\) , and \(\tr(\A\bSigma)=n-1\) . By @thm-qf-chisq (b) the form is noncentral chi-squared with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom and noncentrality \(\bmu\T\A\bmu\) , which is zero exactly when \(\bmu\) is constant. The listing takes \(n=8\) , an autoregressive correlation \(\bSigma=(\rho^{\lvert i-j\rvert})\) with \(\rho=0.6\) , and a linear trend in the mean, for which \(\gamma=4.200\) . Figure 4.3.1 (a) compares \(200{,}000\) simulated values with the \(\chi^2(7,4.200)\) density.

content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n\bigl(\mu\bone,\sigma^2\{(1-\rho)\I+\rho\bone\bone\T\}\bigr)\) with \(-1/(n-1)<\rho<1\) , and let \(\bar{Y}\) and \(S^2\) be the sample mean and variance. Show that \((n-1)S^2/\{\sigma^2(1-\rho)\}\sim\chi^2(n-1)\) and that \(S^2\) is independent of \(\bar{Y}\) . Deduce that \(\sqrt n(\bar{Y}-\mu)/S\) has the law of \(\{(1+(n-1)\rho)/(1-\rho)\}^{1/2}\) times a \(t(n-1)\) variable, and describe what a positive \(\rho\) does to the coverage of the usual \(95\%\) \(t\) interval for \(\mu\) .

title: Theorem 4.3.2 (When a quadratic form is chi-squared)
page: 4.3 When a quadratic form is chi-squared

title: Theorem 4.3.1 (Chi-squared forms in a spherical normal vector)
page: 4.3 When a quadratic form is chi-squared
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\I_n)\) , let \(\A\) be symmetric, and let \(r\ge1\) be an integer and \(\gamma\ge0\) . Then \(\Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r,\gamma)\) if and only if \(\A\) is idempotent with \(\rank(\A)=r\) and \(\gamma=\bmu\T\A\bmu\) .

title: Corollary 4.4.5 (Sample mean and sample variance)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(Y_1,\dots,Y_n\) ( \(n\ge2\) ) be independent \(\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2)\) , with sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) and sample variance \(S^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-\bar{Y})^2\) . Then \(\bar{Y}\) and \(S^2\) are independent, and \(\bar{Y}\sim\Normal(\mu,\sigma^2/n)\) ; \((n-1)S^2/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(n-1)\) ; for any \(\mu_0\) , \(T=\sqrt n(\bar{Y}-\mu_0)/S\sim t(n-1,\delta)\) with \(\delta=\sqrt n(\mu-\mu_0)/\sigma\) . In particular \(T\sim t(n-1)\) when \(\mu=\mu_0\) .

title: Example (Detecting curvature)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) , \(n=15\) , be equally spaced on \([0,1]\) , and suppose \(Y_i=1+0.5x_i+\beta_2x_i^2+\varepsilon_i\) with independent \(\Normal(0,1)\) errors. To test for curvature, compare the straight line ( \(\X_0=[\bone,\x]\) ) with the quadratic ( \(\X=[\bone,\x,\x^2]\) ). The \(F\) statistic has \(1\) and \(12\) degrees of freedom, and the \(5\%\) critical value is \(4.747\) . For \(\beta_2=8.0\) , the listing finds \(\gamma=6.873\) and power \(0.673\) from the noncentral \(F\) , and the rejection rate in \(100{,}000\) simulated data sets is \(0.674\) . The noncentrality has a clear meaning. It is \(\beta_2^2\) times the squared length of the part of \(\x^2\) orthogonal to \(\bone\) and \(\x\) , divided by \(\sigma^2\) . It grows roughly in proportion to \(n\) for a fixed design pattern. Keeping the same design on \([0,1]\) , the smallest \(n\) with power at least \(0.8\) is \(21\) , where \(\gamma=8.97\) . Figure 4.4.1 places the example on the power curve and shows the loss of power when the same noncentrality is spread over more numerator degrees of freedom \(r\) . At \(\gamma=10\) the power is \(0.827\) , \(0.606\) and \(0.421\) for \(r=1,3,6\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: In @exm-qf-drift let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu\bone,\sigma^2\I)\) with \(n\ge3\) . Use @thm-qf-mean-var (d) to show that \(\Cov(S^2,Q)=\Var(S^2)\) , and deduce that \(S^2\) and \(Q\) are dependent with correlation \(\{2(n-1)/(3n-4)\}^{1/2}\) . Which linear forms \(\bm a\T\Y\) are independent of \(Q\) for every mean vector \(\bmu\in\Real^n\) ?

title: Exercise (B4)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Show that \(F_\alpha(r,s)\to\chi^2_\alpha(r)/r\) as \(s\to\infty\) , where \(\chi^2_\alpha(r)\) is the upper \(\alpha\) point of \(\chi^2(r)\) , and that the power \(\Pr\{F(r,s,\gamma)>F_\alpha(r,s)\}\) tends to \(\Pr\{\chi^2(r,\gamma)>\chi^2_\alpha(r)\}\) , the power of the test that knows \(\sigma^2\) .

title: Exercise (B3)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\X\bbeta,\sigma^2\I)\) with \(\X\) of full column rank \(p<n\) , let \(\hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\Y\) , \(\M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\) and \(s^2=\norm{(\I-\M)\Y}^2/(n-p)\) . With \(v_{jj}\) the \(j\) th diagonal entry of \((\X\T\X)^{-1}\) , show that \((\hat{\beta}_j-b)/(s\sqrt{v_{jj}})\sim t\bigl(n-p,(\beta_j-b)/(\sigma\sqrt{v_{jj}})\bigr)\) .

title: Exercise (B2)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) and let \(\A,\B\) be nonnegative definite with \(\bSigma\A\bSigma\B\bSigma=\bm0\) . Show that \(\A\bSigma\B=\bm0\) , so that \(\Y\T\A\Y\) and \(\Y\T\B\Y\) are independent. Show by an example that the implication can fail when \(\A\) is not nonnegative definite.

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_2(\bzero,\I)\) . Show that \(Y_1^2-Y_2^2\) and \(2Y_1Y_2\) are uncorrelated but not independent. Why does @prp-qf-craig-nnd not apply?

title: Proposition 4.4.3 (Necessity for nonnegative definite forms)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bzero,\I)\) and let \(\A,\B\) be nonnegative definite. If \(\Y\T\A\Y\) and \(\Y\T\B\Y\) are independent, then \(\A\B=\bm0\) .

title: Theorem 4.4.1 (Linear and quadratic forms)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) , let \(\B\) be \(m\times n\) and \(\A\) symmetric \(n\times n\) . If \(\B\bSigma\A=\bm0\) , then \(\B\Y\) and \(\Y\T\A\Y\) are independent. Conversely, if \(\B\Y\) and \(\Y\T\A\Y\) are independent for every \(\bmu\in\Real^n\) , with \(\bSigma\) fixed, then \(\B\bSigma\A=\bm0\) .

title: Theorem 4.4.2 (Two quadratic forms)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\bSigma)\) and let \(\A,\B\) be symmetric. If \(\A\bSigma\B=\bm0\) , equivalently \(\B\bSigma\A=\bm0\) , then \(\Y\T\A\Y\) and \(\Y\T\B\Y\) are independent.

title: Theorem 4.4.6 (F statistic for nested subspaces)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\sigma^2\I)\) , and let \(\bP_0\) and \(\bP\) be symmetric idempotent matrices of ranks \(r_0<r<n\) with \(\bP\bP_0=\bP_0\) . Suppose that \(\bP\bmu=\bmu\) . Then \[ F=\frac{\Y\T(\bP-\bP_0)\Y/(r-r_0)}{\Y\T(\I-\bP)\Y/(n-r)} \sim F\Bigl(r-r_0,\;n-r,\;\frac{\norm{(\bP-\bP_0)\bmu}^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr), \] and the noncentrality is zero iff \(\bP_0\bmu=\bmu\) .

title: Theorem 4.4.4 (Independent projections)
page: 4.4 Independence of quadratic forms and linear forms

title: Example (The one-way layout)
content: Let observations fall into \(g\) groups of sizes \(n_1,\dots,n_g\) , with \(Y_{\ell j}\) independent \(\Normal(\mu_\ell,\sigma^2)\) . Let \(\M\) replace each observation by its group mean, and \(\bP_1=n^{-1}\bone\bone\T\) by the grand mean. Then \[ \I=\bP_1+(\M-\bP_1)+(\I-\M) \] splits \(\norm{\Y}^2\) into \(n\bar{Y}^2\) , the between-group sum of squares \(\sum_\ell n_\ell(\bar{Y}_\ell-\bar{Y})^2\) and the within-group sum of squares \(\sum_{\ell,j}(Y_{\ell j}-\bar{Y}_\ell)^2\) . The three matrices are symmetric with ranks \(1\) , \(g-1\) and \(n-g\) , which add to \(n\) . Cochran’s theorem needs nothing more. The three sums of squares, divided by \(\sigma^2\) , are independent noncentral chi-squared variables. Their noncentralities are \(n\bar{\mu}^2/\sigma^2\) , \(\sum_\ell n_\ell(\mu_\ell-\bar{\mu})^2/\sigma^2\) with \(\bar{\mu}=\sum_\ell n_\ell\mu_\ell/n\) , and \(0\) . The last is zero because \(\M\bmu=\bmu\) . The ratio of the between and within mean squares is \(F(g-1,n-g,\gamma)\) by @thm-qf-nested-f , and it is central iff all group means are equal. The script uses \(g=3\) groups of sizes \(3, 5, 4\) , means \(2, 3, 1.5\) , and \(\sigma=1\) , and draws \(200{,}000\) data sets. Table 4.5.1 compares the theoretical means \(r_i+\gamma_i\) and variances \(2r_i+4\gamma_i\) with the simulated ones. The largest absolute correlation between the three sums of squares is \(0.0013\) . As a check that goes beyond correlation, the proportion of data sets in which both the between and the within sums of squares exceed their medians is \(0.2497\) , against \(0.25\) for independent variables.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Let \(\A_1=\diag(2,0)\) and \(\A_2=\diag(-1,1)\) , so that \(\A_1+\A_2=\I_2\) . Which hypotheses of @thm-qf-cochran fail, and what are the laws of the two forms when \(\Y\sim\Normal_2(\bzero,\I)\) ?

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bzero,\I)\) , and \(Q=Q_1+Q_2\) with \(Q=\Y\T\A\Y\sim\chi^2(r)\) , \(Q_1=\Y\T\A_1\Y\sim\chi^2(r_1)\) and \(Q_2=\Y\T\A_2\Y\) for a nonnegative definite \(\A_2\) . Show that \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are independent and \(Q_2\sim\chi^2(r-r_1)\) .

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Let \(\bP_1,\dots,\bP_m\) be symmetric idempotent with \(\C(\bP_1)\subset\C(\bP_2)\subset\dots\subset\C(\bP_m)\) , and put \(\bP_0=\bm0\) , \(\bP_{m+1}=\I\) . Show that the matrices \(\bP_i-\bP_{i-1}\) , \(i=1,\dots,m+1\) , satisfy the conditions of @thm-qf-cochran , so that the sequential sums of squares \(\norm{(\bP_i-\bP_{i-1})\Y}^2\) are independent noncentral chi-squared variables when \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\sigma^2\I)\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
content: A two-way layout has one observation \(Y_{ij}\) for each of \(a\) rows and \(b\) columns. Write \(\norm{\Y}^2\) as the sum of the grand-mean, row, column and residual sums of squares, identify the four matrices, and use @thm-qf-cochran to show that under \(Y_{ij}\sim\Normal(\mu+\alpha_i+\beta_j,\sigma^2)\) independently the four sums of squares are independent, with degrees of freedom \(1\) , \(a-1\) , \(b-1\) and \((a-1)(b-1)\) .

title: Theorem 4.5.2 (Cochran)
content: Let \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\bmu,\sigma^2\I)\) , and let \(\A_1,\dots,\A_k\) be symmetric with ranks \(r_1,\dots,r_k\) , whose sum \(\A=\sum_i\A_i\) is idempotent of rank \(r\) (for example \(\A=\I\) , \(r=n\) ). The following are equivalent: the forms \(\Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2\) are mutually independent, and \(\Y\T\A_i\Y/\sigma^2\sim\chi^2(r_i,\bmu\T\A_i\bmu/\sigma^2)\) for each \(i\) ; \(r_1+\dots+r_k=r\) ; each \(\A_i\) is idempotent; \(\A_i\A_j=\bm0\) for all \(i\ne j\) .

title: Theorem 4.5.1 (Cochran, algebraic form)
content: Let \(\A_1,\dots,\A_k\) be symmetric \(n\times n\) matrices and \(\A=\sum_i\A_i\) . Consider each \(\A_i\) is idempotent; \(\A_i\A_j=\bm0\) for all \(i\ne j\) ; \(\A\) is idempotent; \(\rank(\A)=\sum_i\rank(\A_i)\) . Then any two of (a), (b), (c) imply all four, and (c) together with (d) implies all four.

title: Definition 6.1.1 (Least squares)
page: 6.1 Least squares as a nearest-point problem
content: A vector \(\hbeta\in\Real^p\) is a least squares estimate of \(\bbeta\) if \[ \norm{\y-\X\hbeta} \le \norm{\y-\X\bb} \qquad\text{for every } \bb\in\Real^p. \] The vector \(\hY=\X\hbeta\) is the fitted value vector, and \(\he=\y-\hY\) is the residual vector.

title: Example (Three observations)
page: 6.1 Least squares as a nearest-point problem
content:
Take responses \(\y=(1,4,2)\T\) at regressor values \(\x=(0,1,3)\T\) , with an intercept, so that \(\X=[ one,\x]\) . The least squares fit (computed by the listing below) is \[ \hY = (2.143,\ 2.286,\ 2.571)\T,\qquad \he = (-1.143,\ 1.714,\ -0.571)\T, \] with intercept \(2.143\) and slope \(0.143\) . Two facts stand out. First, the residual is orthogonal to both columns of \(\X\) : the entries of \(\he\) sum to zero, and \(\x\T\he = 0\) . Second, the squared lengths add: \[ 
orm{\y}^2=21.000 = 16.429 + 4.571 = 
orm{\hY}^2+
orm{\he}^2 . \] Figure 6.1.1 shows the configuration. The fitted vector is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from \(\y\) to the plane.

title: Corollary 6.2.4
content: For any \(n\times p\) matrix \(\A\) : \(\Null(\A\T\A)=\Null(\A)\) ; \(\C(\A\T\A)=\C(\A\T)\) and \(\C(\A\A\T)=\C(\A)\) ; \(\rank(\A\T\A)=\rank(\A\A\T)=\rank(\A)\) ; \(\C(\A)\perpc=\Null(\A\T)\) and \(\Real^p=\C(\A\T)\dirsum\Null(\A)\) .

title: Definition 6.2.1 (Orthogonal complement)
content: The orthogonal complement of a subspace \(\mathcal S\subseteq\Real^n\) is \[ \mathcal S\perpc=\{\bv\in\Real^n:\bv\T\bu=0\text{ for all }\bu\in\mathcal S\}. \]

title: Example (A rank-deficient layout)
content: Suppose \(n\) observations fall into \(g\) groups and \(\X=[\bone,\,\bz_1,\dots,\bz_g]\) , where \(\bz_k\) is the indicator of group \(k\) . Since \(\bz_1+\dots+\bz_g=\bone\) , the vector \((1,-1,\dots,-1)\T\) lies in \(\Null(\X)\) . The \(g\) indicators are linearly independent (their supports are disjoint), so \(\rank(\X)=g\) while \(p=g+1\) . By @eq-proj-rank-nullity , \(\Null(\X)\) is exactly the line spanned by \((1,-1,\dots,-1)\T\) . The model space \(\C(\X)=\C([\bz_1,\dots,\bz_g])\) is the set of vectors that are constant within groups.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Show that \(\C(\A\B)\subseteq\C(\A)\) , and deduce \(\rank(\A\B)\le\min\{\rank(\A),\rank(\B)\}\) . Show that \(\C(\A\B)=\C(\A)\) whenever \(\B\) has full row rank.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Show that \(\mathcal S\perpc\) is a subspace for any set \(\mathcal S\) (not necessarily a subspace), and that \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal T\) implies \(\mathcal T\perpc\subseteq\mathcal S\perpc\) . Show that \(\mathcal S\perpc=\spn(\mathcal S)\perpc\) .

title: Exercise (C1)
content: For subspaces \(\mathcal S,\mathcal T\subseteq\Real^n\) , prove \(\dim(\mathcal S+\mathcal T)=\dim\mathcal S+\dim\mathcal T-\dim(\mathcal S\cap\mathcal T)\) . Use it to show that two \(r\) -dimensional subspaces of \(\Real^n\) with \(2r>n\) must share a nonzero vector.

title: Exercise (B1)
content: A one-way layout has three groups of sizes \(2,2,1\) and model matrix \(\X=[\bone,\bz_1,\bz_2,\bz_3]\) . Find bases for \(\C(\X)\) , \(\Null(\X)\) , \(\C(\X\T)\) and \(\C(\X)\perpc\) , and check that the dimensions agree with @eq-proj-rank-nullity and @thm-proj-direct-sum .

title: Lemma 6.2.5
content: For subspaces \(\mathcal S_1,\mathcal S_2\subseteq\Real^n\) , \[ (\mathcal S_1+\mathcal S_2)\perpc=\mathcal S_1\perpc\cap\mathcal S_2\perpc \qquad\text{and}\qquad (\mathcal S_1\cap\mathcal S_2)\perpc=\mathcal S_1\perpc+\mathcal S_2\perpc . \]

title: Lemma 6.2.1
content: For any \(n\times p\) matrix \(\A\) , \[ \Null(\A\T)=\C(\A)\perpc \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Null(\A)=\C(\A\T)\perpc . \]

title: Proposition 6.2.2 (Gram–Schmidt)
content: Let \(\bv_1,\dots,\bv_k\) be linearly independent. Define recursively \[ \bw_j=\bv_j-\sum_{i<j}(\bu_i\T\bv_j)\,\bu_i,\qquad \bu_j=\bw_j/\norm{\bw_j},\qquad j=1,\dots,k. \] Then each \(\bw_j\neq\bzero\) . The vectors \(\bu_1,\dots,\bu_k\) are orthonormal, and \(\spn(\bu_1,\dots,\bu_j)=\spn(\bv_1,\dots,\bv_j)\) for every \(j\) .

title: Theorem 6.2.3 (Orthogonal decomposition)
content: For every subspace \(\mathcal S\subseteq\Real^n\) , \[ \Real^n=\mathcal S\dirsum\mathcal S\perpc, \qquad \dim\mathcal S+\dim\mathcal S\perpc=n, \qquad (\mathcal S\perpc)\perpc=\mathcal S . \] Hence every \(\y\in\Real^n\) can be written uniquely as \(\y=\bu+\bv\) with \(\bu\in\mathcal S\) and \(\bv\perp\mathcal S\) .

title: Definition 6.3.2 (Generalized inverse)
content: A generalized inverse of an \(m\times k\) matrix \(\A\) is any \(k\times m\) matrix \(\A\ginv\) such that \(\A\A\ginv\A=\A\) .

title: Definition 6.3.1 (Orthogonal projection matrix)
content: The orthogonal projection onto a subspace \(\mathcal S\) is the unique \(n\times n\) matrix \(\bP_{\mathcal S}\) such that, for every \(\y\) , \(\bP_{\mathcal S}\y\in\mathcal S\) and \(\y-\bP_{\mathcal S}\y\perp\mathcal S\) . When \(\mathcal S=\C(\X)\) for the model matrix of a linear model, we write \(\M=\bP_{\C(\X)}\) .

title: Example (Projections onto a line)
content: For \(\mathcal S=\spn(\bv)\) with \(\bv\ne\bzero\) , the single vector \(\bv/\norm{\bv}\) is an orthonormal basis, so \[ \bP_{\mathcal S}=\frac{\bv\bv\T}{\bv\T\bv}, \qquad \bP_{\mathcal S}\y=\frac{\bv\T\y}{\bv\T\bv}\,\bv . \] With \(\bv=\bone\) this gives \(\bP=n^{-1}\bone\bone\T\) , the matrix with every entry \(1/n\) , and \(\bP\y=\bar y\,\bone\) . The sample mean is a projection : fitting the intercept-only model replaces every observation by \(\bar y\) , and the residuals \(y_i-\bar y\) form a vector in \(\bone\perpc\) , the set of vectors whose entries sum to zero.

title: Example (The one-way layout)
content: In the setting of @exm-proj-oneway-rank , sort the observations by group and let group \(k\) have \(n_k\) members. The model space is spanned by the orthogonal vectors \(\bz_1,\dots,\bz_g\) , so by @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula with \(\bu_k=\bz_k/\sqrt{n_k}\) , \[ \M=\sum_{k=1}^g\frac{\bz_k\bz_k\T}{n_k} =\begin{pmatrix} n_1^{-1}\bone_{n_1}\bone_{n_1}\T & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & n_g^{-1}\bone_{n_g}\bone_{n_g}\T \end{pmatrix}, \] a block-diagonal matrix of within-group averaging operators. \(\M\y\) replaces each observation by its group mean. The intercept column adds nothing to \(\C(\X)\) , so it does not appear, and \(\tr(\M)=\sum_k n_k/n_k=g=\rank(\X)\) . We got here without a generalized inverse. @thm-proj-M-formula guarantees that any generalized inverse of the singular \((g+1)\times(g+1)\) matrix \(\X\T\X\) produces this same matrix. Section 6.4 checks this numerically.

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Show that \(\M\) is the only \(n\times n\) matrix \(\bP\) satisfying \(\bP\X=\X\) , \(\bP\T=\bP\) and \(\rank(\bP)=\rank(\X)\) . Is the rank condition necessary? Is symmetry?

title: Exercise (A3)
content: Let \(\bP\) be an orthogonal projection and \(a,b\) real numbers. Show that the eigenvalues of \(a\bP+b\I\) are \(b\) and \(a+b\) . Show that when \(b\ne0\) and \(a+b\ne0\) , \[ (a\bP+b\I)^{-1}=\frac1b\Bigl(\I-\frac{a}{a+b}\bP\Bigr). \] Use this to invert the equicorrelation matrix \((1-\rho)\I+\rho\bone\bone\T\) .

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Let \(\G_0\) be a generalized inverse of \(\A\) . Show that \(\G_0+(\I-\G_0\A)\bU+\V(\I-\A\G_0)\) is a generalized inverse of \(\A\) for all conformable \(\bU,\V\) . Show that every generalized inverse \(\G\) of \(\A\) has this form. Hint: take \(\bU=\G-\G_0\) and \(\V=\G_0\A(\G-\G_0)\) , and use \(\A(\G-\G_0)\A=\bzero\) . Conclude that a matrix has a unique generalized inverse iff it is square and nonsingular.

title: Exercise (A4)
content: Show that if \(\G\) is a generalized inverse of the symmetric matrix \(\X\T\X\) , then so is \(\G\T\) , and so is \(\G\X\T\X\G\T\) . Which of the four Penrose conditions does the last one satisfy?

title: Exercise (B3)
content: Using the singular value decomposition, show that \((\X\T\X)^+\X\T=\X^+\) and \(\X\X^+=\M\) . Show also that \(\X^+=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\) when \(\X\) has full column rank.

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Let \(\bP_1,\bP_2\) be orthogonal projections. Show that \(\bP_1\bP_2\) is an orthogonal projection iff \(\bP_1\bP_2=\bP_2\bP_1\) , and that in this case it projects onto \(\C(\bP_1)\cap\C(\bP_2)\) . Hint: for the range, show \(\bP_1\bP_2\bu=\bu\) iff \(\bu\) lies in both subspaces.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Let \(\mathcal S=\spn\{(1,1,0)\T,(0,1,1)\T\}\) . Compute \(\bP_{\mathcal S}\) in two ways: by Gram–Schmidt and @prp-proj-orthonormal-formula , and by @thm-proj-M-formula . Verify symmetry, idempotence and \(\tr\bP_{\mathcal S}=2\) . Find \(\mathcal S\perpc\) and check that \(\I-\bP_{\mathcal S}\) projects onto it.

title: Exercise (A2)
content: Show that a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues all lie in \(\{0,1\}\) is an orthogonal projection. Give a non-symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix with eigenvalues \(0\) and \(1\) that is not idempotent, and one that is idempotent.

title: Lemma 6.3.6
content: Let \(\X\) be \(n\times p\) and let \(\G\) be any generalized inverse of \(\X\T\X\) . Then: \(\X\G\X\T\X=\X\) and \(\X\T\X\G\X\T=\X\T\) ; \(\X\G\X\T\) does not depend on the choice of generalized inverse; \(\X\G\X\T\) is symmetric, even when \(\G\) is not.

title: Proposition 6.3.5 (Existence)
content: Every matrix has a generalized inverse. If \(\A\) has rank \(r\) and is permuted so that \[ \A=\begin{pmatrix}\A_{11}&\A_{12}\\\A_{21}&\A_{22}\end{pmatrix} \] with \(\A_{11}\) an \(r\times r\) nonsingular block, then \(\A\ginv=\begin{pmatrix}\A_{11}^{-1}&\bzero\\\bzero&\bzero\end{pmatrix}\) (permuted back) is a generalized inverse.

title: Proposition 6.3.2
content: Let the columns of the \(n\times r\) matrix \(\Q\) be an orthonormal basis for \(\mathcal S\) , so that \(\Q\T\Q=\I_r\) . Then \[ \bP_{\mathcal S}=\Q\Q\T=\sum_{i=1}^r\bu_i\bu_i\T, \] where \(\bu_1,\dots,\bu_r\) are the columns of \(\Q\) .

title: Proposition 6.3.4 (Spectrum, rank and trace)
content: Let \(\bP\) be the orthogonal projection onto an \(r\) -dimensional subspace \(\mathcal S\) . Then: every eigenvalue of \(\bP\) is \(0\) or \(1\) , and \(1\) has multiplicity \(r\) ; \(\rank(\bP)=\tr(\bP)=r\) ; \(\bP\bv=\bv\) iff \(\bv\in\mathcal S\) , and \(\bP\bv=\bzero\) iff \(\bv\in\mathcal S\perpc\) ; \(\bv\T\bP\bv=\norm{\bP\bv}^2\le\norm{\bv}^2\) , so \(\bP\) and \(\I-\bP\) are nonnegative definite.

title: Theorem 6.3.7
content: For any \(n\times p\) matrix \(\X\) and any generalized inverse \((\X\T\X)\ginv\) , \[ \M=\X(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T \] is the orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\X)\) . In particular \(\rank(\M)=\tr(\M)=\rank(\X)\) . If \(\X\) has full column rank, \(\M=\X(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\) .

title: Theorem 6.3.1 (Projection theorem)
content:
Let \(\mathcal S\) be a subspace of \(\Real^n\) and \(\y\in\Real^n\) . There is exactly one \(\hat{\y}\in\mathcal S\) such that \[ 
orm{\y-\hat{\y}}\le
orm{\y- u}\qquad	ext{for all } u\in\mathcal S . \] It is the unique \(\hat{\y}\in\mathcal S\) with \(\y-\hat{\y}\perp\mathcal S\) . Moreover, for every \( u\in\mathcal S\) , \[ 
orm{\y- u}^2=
orm{\y-\hat{\y}}^2+
orm{\hat{\y}- u}^2 . \] {#eq-proj-distance-split}

title: Theorem 6.3.8
content: Let \(\bP_1,\bP_2\) be orthogonal projections. Then \(\bP_1+\bP_2\) is an orthogonal projection iff \(\bP_1\bP_2=\bzero\) , that is, iff \(\C(\bP_1)\perp\C(\bP_2)\) . In that case it projects onto \(\C(\bP_1)\dirsum\C(\bP_2)\) .

title: Theorem 6.3.3
content: An \(n\times n\) matrix \(\bP\) is the orthogonal projection onto some subspace iff \(\bP\T=\bP\) and \(\bP^2=\bP\) . In that case the subspace is \(\C(\bP)\) , and \(\I-\bP\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\bP)\perpc\) .

title: Example (Four answers, one fit)
content: Nine observations fall in three groups of sizes \(3,2,4\) with group means \(5.700\) , \(7.800\) and \(4.300\) . The model matrix \(\X=[\bone,\bz_1,\bz_2,\bz_3]\) has \(p=4\) columns and rank \(3\) , so \(\X\T\X\) is singular. We compute \(\hbeta=\G\X\T\y\) for four generalized inverses \(\G\) of \(\X\T\X\) : the Moore–Penrose inverse; the inverse obtained by deleting the intercept row and column ( @prp-proj-ginverse-exists ); the one obtained by deleting the first group’s row and column; and a deliberately strange, non-symmetric one built from the general formula of @exr-proj-all-ginverses . Generalized inverse \(\hat{\beta}_0\) \(\hat{\beta}_1\) \(\hat{\beta}_2\) \(\hat{\beta}_3\) \(\hat{\beta}_1-\hat{\beta}_2\) \(\max\lvert\M-\M_{\text{MP}}\rvert\) Moore–Penrose 4.450 1.250 3.350 -0.150 -2.100 0 drop intercept 0.000 5.700 7.800 4.300 -2.100 \(1.1\times 10^{-16}\) drop group 1 5.700 0.000 2.100 -1.400 -2.100 \(1.1\times 10^{-16}\) random -9.102 14.802 16.902 13.402 -2.100 \(1.8\times 10^{-15}\) The coefficient vectors disagree wildly, including in sign. Yet each produces the same projection matrix up to rounding error, and hence the same fitted values (the group means) and residuals. The difference \(\hat{\beta}_1-\hat{\beta}_2\) is the same in every row, and so is \(\hat{\beta}_0+\hat{\beta}_k\) for each \(k\) . Individual coefficients are not. The trace of \(\M\) is \(3.000\) , the rank of \(\X\) .

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Suppose \(\X\T\y\neq\bzero\) . Show that every least squares estimate \(\bb\) can be written as \(\G\X\T\y\) for some generalized inverse \(\G\) of \(\A=\X\T\X\) . Hint: with \(\bm c=\X\T\y\) , try \(\G=\G_0+(\bb-\G_0\bm c)\bm c\T/(\bm c\T\bm c)\) . What goes wrong when \(\X\T\y=\bzero\) ?

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Suppose \(\E(\Y)=\X\bbeta\) and \(\Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\I\) . Show that \(\E(\hY)=\X\bbeta\) , \(\Cov(\hY)=\sigma^2\M\) , \(\Cov(\he)=\sigma^2(\I-\M)\) and \(\Cov(\hY,\he)=\bzero\) . Which of these statements survive when \(\Cov(\Y)=\sigma^2\V\) for a general positive definite \(\V\) ?

title: Exercise (A2)
content: Show that the residuals sum to zero whenever \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) , even if no column of \(\X\) is constant. Give an example of a model without such a column in which this happens, and one in which the residuals do not sum to zero.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Let \(\rank(\X)=r<p\) and let \(\bm C\) be a \((p-r)\times p\) matrix. Show that the constrained problem “minimize \(\norm{\y-\X\bb}\) subject to \(\bm C\bb=\bzero\) ” has a unique solution for every \(\y\) , and that its fitted values are \(\M\y\) , iff \(\rank\begin{psmallmatrix}\X\\\bm C\end{psmallmatrix}=p\) . Show that the condition implies \(\C(\bm C\T)\cap\C(\X\T)=\{\bzero\}\) , and interpret: the constraints must not restrict any estimable function.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For @exm-proj-three-points , write out the \(3\times3\) matrix \(\M\) with exact fractional entries, verify \(\tr\M=2\) , and recover the fitted values and residuals quoted in the text.

title: Proposition 6.4.3
content:
For any data vector \(\y\) : \(\X\T\he= zero\) and \(\hY\T\he=0\) ; if \( one\in\C(\X)\) (for example, the model has an intercept), then \(\sum_i\hat{\varepsilon}_i=0\) and the mean of the fitted values is \( ar y\) ; \(
orm{\y}^2=
orm{\hY}^2+
orm{\he}^2\) ; \(
orm{\he}^2=\y\T(\I-\M)\y\) and \(
orm{\hY}^2=\y\T\M\y\) ; if \(\y=\X beta+ e\) for some \( beta\) , then \(\hY=\X beta+\M e\) and \(\he=(\I-\M) e\) .

title: Theorem 6.4.4
content: For \(\blambda\in\Real^p\) , the value \(\blambda\T\hbeta\) is the same for every least squares estimate \(\hbeta\) (and every \(\y\) ) iff \(\blambda\in\C(\X\T)\) , that is, iff \(\blambda\T=\bm{\rho}\T\X\) for some \(\bm\rho\in\Real^n\) . In that case \(\blambda\T\hbeta=\bm\rho\T\M\y\) .

title: Theorem 6.4.1 (Least squares is projection)
content: A vector \(\hbeta\) is a least squares estimate of \(\bbeta\) iff \[ \X\hbeta=\M\y . \] Consequently the fitted values \(\hY=\M\y\) and residuals \(\he=(\I-\M)\y\) are the same for every least squares estimate.

title: Theorem 6.4.2 (Normal equations)
content: The normal equations \[ \X\T\X\bb=\X\T\y \] {#eq-proj-normal-equations} are consistent for every \(\y\) , and their solutions are exactly the least squares estimates. One solution is \(\hbeta=(\X\T\X)\ginv\X\T\y\) , for any generalized inverse, and the set of all solutions is \[ \hbeta+\Null(\X)=\{\hbeta+\bv:\X\bv=\bzero\}. \] In particular, the least squares estimate is unique iff \(\rank(\X)=p\) , and then \(\hbeta=(\X\T\X)^{-1}\X\T\y\) .

title: Example (Order matters)
content: For the state data of @exm-proj-fwl-crime , enter the three regressors after the intercept in two different orders. The listing computes each squared length \(\norm{(\M_j-\M_{j-1})\y}^2\) directly from the projections. Order A Order B poverty 102.49 single-parent 162.84 single-parent 80.04 urban 3.59 urban 0.27 poverty 16.37 residual 101.96 residual 101.96 Entered first, poverty accounts for \(102.49\) of the corrected total sum of squares \(284.76\) . Entered last, it accounts for only \(16.37\) . The residual sum of squares, and the total explained by all three regressors together ( \(182.80\) ), do not depend on the order, because the final subspace does not. The individual pieces do depend on the order, because the intermediate subspaces differ. Poverty and single parenthood are correlated, so whichever enters first takes the variation they share. The piece for the last regressor is the only one with an order-free meaning. By @thm-proj-fwl , it is the squared length of the projection of \(\y\) onto the part of that regressor orthogonal to all the others.

title: Example (Intercept inside simple regression)
content: Let \(\X_0=\bone\) and \(\X=[\bone,\x]\) with \(\x\) not constant. Then \(\C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X)\) is spanned by the centred regressor \(\x-\bar x\bone=(\I-n^{-1}\bone\bone\T)\x\) , which lies in \(\C(\X)\) and is orthogonal to \(\bone\) . By @exm-proj-line , \[ \M-\Mo=\frac{(\x-\bar x\bone)(\x-\bar x\bone)\T}{S_{xx}}, \qquad S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2, \] and so \[ \M\y=\bar y\bone+\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}(\x-\bar x\bone), \qquad S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y). \] Reading off coordinates, the slope is \(S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and the intercept is \(\bar y-\bar x\,S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) . These are the familiar formulas, obtained without solving any equations, and the decomposition @eq-proj-three-way becomes \[ \sum_i y_i^2 = n\bar y^2+\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}+\text{SSE}. \]

title: Example (Additive two-factor model, one observation per cell)
content: Let factor \(A\) have \(a\) levels and factor \(B\) have \(b\) levels, with one observation \(y_{ij}\) for each of the \(n=ab\) combinations. Let \(\bP_A\) project onto vectors that depend only on the \(A\) level, so \(\bP_A\y\) has entries \(\bar y_{i\cdot}\) , and define \(\bP_B\) similarly. Let \(\bP_0=n^{-1}\bone\bone\T\) . Both \(\C(\bP_A)\) and \(\C(\bP_B)\) contain \(\bone\) , so \(\bP_A\bP_0=\bP_B\bP_0=\bP_0\) by @thm-proj-nested . The crucial computation is \(\bP_A\bP_B\) . Averaging over \(j\) with \(i\) fixed a vector that depends only on \(j\) gives the overall average of that vector. So for every \(\y\) the entries of \(\bP_A(\bP_B\y)\) are all equal to \(b^{-1}\sum_j\bar y_{\cdot j}=\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}\) . Therefore \[ \bP_A\bP_B=\bP_0, \] and so \((\bP_A-\bP_0)(\bP_B-\bP_0)=\bP_0-\bP_0-\bP_0+\bP_0=\bzero\) . The two centred factor spaces are orthogonal. By @thm-proj-sum , the additive model space has projection \(\bP_0+(\bP_A-\bP_0)+(\bP_B-\bP_0)=\bP_A+\bP_B-\bP_0\) , and \[ \I=\bP_0+(\bP_A-\bP_0)+(\bP_B-\bP_0)+(\I-\bP_A-\bP_B+\bP_0) \] is an orthogonal decomposition with ranks \(1\) , \(a-1\) , \(b-1\) and \((a-1)(b-1)\) . The residual projection sends \(y_{ij}\) to \(y_{ij}-\bar y_{i\cdot}-\bar y_{\cdot j}+\bar y_{\cdot\cdot}\) . The key step used the fact that every \(A\) level appears with every \(B\) level equally often. If cells are missing or unequally replicated, \(\bP_A\bP_B\neq\bP_0\) , the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and the sum of squares for \(A\) depends on whether \(B\) was fitted first. Chapter 17 is about that situation.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: In the model \(\E(\Y)=\beta_0\bone+\beta_1\x_1+\beta_2\x_2+\beta_3\x_3\) with full-rank \(\X\) , the hypothesis \(\beta_2=\beta_3\) defines a reduced model with model matrix \(\X_0=[\bone,\x_1,\x_2+\x_3]\) . Show that the test space \(\C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X)\) is spanned by \((\I-\Mo)\x_2\) , and that \((\I-\Mo)\x_2=-(\I-\Mo)\x_3\) . Verify that this agrees with @thm-proj-constraint-space for a suitable \(\bm P\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
content: With \(\C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X)\) , show that \(\text{SSE}_0-\text{SSE}=\norm{\hY-\hY_0}^2\) , the squared distance between the two fitted vectors.

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Extend @exm-proj-two-factor to \(m\ge2\) observations in every cell and a model with interaction. Find five mutually orthogonal projections summing to \(\I\) , corresponding to the grand mean, factor \(A\) , factor \(B\) , the interaction, and within-cell error, and find their ranks. Describe the action of each on \(\y\) in terms of cell, row, column and grand means.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Construct the projections \(\bP_A\) , \(\bP_B\) and \(\bP_0\) of @exm-proj-two-factor for \(a=3\) , \(b=2\) and verify \(\bP_A\bP_B=\bP_0\) numerically. Delete one observation and recompute. Show that the centred factor spaces are no longer orthogonal, and find the largest entry of \((\bP_A-\bP_0)(\bP_B-\bP_0)\) .

title: Theorem 6.5.2
content: Let \(\M\) project onto \(\C(\X)\) and let \(\bm P\) be an \(n\times q\) matrix. If \(\mathcal S_0=\C(\X)\cap\Null(\bm P\T)\) , then \[ \mathcal S_0\perpc\cap\C(\X)=\C(\M\bm P). \] Hence the projection onto \(\mathcal S_0\) is \(\M-\bP_{\C(\M\bm P)}\) , and \(\dim\mathcal S_0=r-\rank(\M\bm P)\) .

title: Theorem 6.5.1 (Nested projections)
content: If \(\C(\X_0)\subseteq\C(\X)\) , then: \(\M\Mo=\Mo\M=\Mo\) ; \(\M-\Mo\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\X_0)\perpc\cap\C(\X)\) , the orthogonal complement of \(\C(\X_0)\) within \(\C(\X)\) ; \(\rank(\M-\Mo)=r-r_0\) ; \((\I-\Mo)-(\I-\M)=\M-\Mo\) , and \(\Mo(\M-\Mo)=(\M-\Mo)(\I-\M)=\bzero\) .

title: Example (Poverty and murder rates)
content: For the \(50\) US states in 2009, regress the murder rate (per 100,000) on the poverty rate, the percentage of single-parent households, and the percentage of the population living in urban areas, with an intercept. The coefficient of poverty is \(0.2538\) . On its own, a simple regression of murder rate on poverty has slope \(0.4706\) , nearly twice as large. Poverty and single parenthood are correlated, and the simple regression gives poverty credit for part of their shared association. Figure 6.6.1 shows both regressions. Panel (b) is an added-variable plot : the residual of murder rate after regression on the other two regressors and the intercept, against the corresponding residual of poverty. By FWL its least squares slope is exactly the multiple-regression coefficient. The listing confirms the equality to machine precision. The standard error of the coefficient in the full model is \(0.0934\) . Fitting the residualized regression naively gives \(0.0905\) , smaller by the factor \(1.0321\) , which is \(\sqrt{(n-1)/(n-4)}\) as predicted.

title: Example (Grunfeld’s investment data)
content: Grunfeld’s classic panel follows \(11\) US firms for \(20\) years, giving \(n=220\) observations of gross investment, market value and capital stock. With a separate intercept for each firm, the coefficients of value and capital are \(0.1101\) and \(0.3100\) . The same numbers come from demeaning every variable within firm and fitting two columns. Ignoring the firms altogether (one common intercept) gives \(0.1145\) and \(0.2275\) instead. That comparison uses variation between firms, of the sort “large firms invest more”, which the within estimator deliberately discards.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Refit the model of @exm-proj-fwl-crime with the District of Columbia included. How does the poverty coefficient change? Draw the added-variable plot and locate the District. Relate what you see to its leverage ( @exm-proj-leverage ).

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Drop the full-rank assumption in @thm-proj-fwl . Show that \(\bb_1\) solves the normal equations of the regression of \(\tilde{\y}\) on \(\tilde{\X}_1\) iff there exists \(\bb_2\) such that \((\bb_1\T,\bb_2\T)\T\) is a least squares estimate in the full model.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: In @thm-proj-fwl , regressing \(\y\) (not \(\tilde{\y}\) ) on \(\tilde{\X}_1\) gives the coefficient \(\hbeta_1\) . Show that its residual vector is \((\I-\M)\y+\M_2\y\) , so the residuals are generally wrong even though the coefficient is right.

title: Exercise (B3)
content: For a single regressor \(\x_j\) , the partial correlation of \(\y\) and \(\x_j\) given the other regressors is the sample correlation of \(\tilde{\y}\) and \(\tilde{\x}_j\) (both residualized on \(\X_{(j)}\) , which contains \(\bone\) ). Let \(t=\hat{\beta}_j/\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)\) with \(\text{se}(\hat{\beta}_j)^2=\text{SSE}/\bigl[(n-p)\norm{\tilde{\x}_j}^2\bigr]\) . Show that the squared partial correlation equals \(t^2/(t^2+n-p)\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Let \(\x_j\) be a column of \(\X\) , let \(\X_{(j)}\) be \(\X\) with that column removed, and assume \(\bone\in\C(\X_{(j)})\) . Show that \(\norm{(\I-\M_{(j)})\x_j}^2=S_{jj}(1-R_j^2)\) , where \(R_j^2\) is the \(R^2\) from regressing \(\x_j\) on \(\X_{(j)}\) . Deduce @eq-proj-vif-preview .

title: Lemma 6.6.1 (Orthogonalizing a partitioned model space)
content: Under the assumptions above: \(\C(\X)=\C(\X_2)\dirsum\C(\tilde{\X}_1)\) , and the two summands are orthogonal; \(\tilde{\X}_1\) has full column rank; \(\M=\M_2+\tilde{\M}_1\) , where \(\tilde{\M}_1=\tilde{\X}_1(\tilde{\X}_1\T\tilde{\X}_1)^{-1}\tilde{\X}_1\T\) .

title: Theorem 6.6.2 (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)
content: Let \(\hbeta=(\hbeta_1\T,\hbeta_2\T)\T\) be the least squares estimate in the full model. Then: \(\hbeta_1=(\tilde{\X}_1\T\tilde{\X}_1)^{-1}\tilde{\X}_1\T\tilde{\y} =(\tilde{\X}_1\T\tilde{\X}_1)^{-1}\tilde{\X}_1\T\y\) . So \(\hbeta_1\) is the coefficient from regressing \(\tilde{\y}\) (or \(\y\) itself) on \(\tilde{\X}_1\) ; the residual vector from regressing \(\tilde{\y}\) on \(\tilde{\X}_1\) equals the residual vector \((\I-\M)\y\) of the full model; \(\hbeta_2=(\X_2\T\X_2)^{-1}\X_2\T(\y-\X_1\hbeta_1)\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: A factor with three levels is coded with an intercept and indicators for levels 2 and 3. Write down the matrices \(\bT\) and \(\bS\) of @thm-proj-reparam that convert to the coding in which level 3, rather than level 1, is the omitted baseline, and to sum-to-zero effect coding. Express each new coefficient in terms of the old ones.

title: Exercise (A2)
content: Show that, for a model with \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) , \(R^2\) is unchanged when \(\y\) is replaced by \(a\bone+b\y\) with \(b\ne0\) , and when any column of \(\X\) is replaced by an affine function of itself. Is it unchanged when a regressor is replaced by its logarithm?

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Suppose \(\Y\sim\Normal_n(\mu\bone,\sigma^2\I)\) and \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) with \(\rank(\X)=r\) . Using the results of Chapter 4 , show that \(R^2\sim\mathrm{Beta}\bigl((r-1)/2,(n-r)/2\bigr)\) , so that \(\E(R^2)=(r-1)/(n-1)\) even though no regressor is related to the response. Use this to motivate the adjusted \(R^2=1-(1-R^2)(n-1)/(n-r)\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Show that if \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) then \(R_0^2=\norm{\hY}^2/\norm{\y}^2=(n\bar y^2+\text{SSR})/(n\bar y^2+\text{SST})\ge R^2\) . Construct a data set and a model without an intercept for which \(R_0^2>0.95\) but the model’s residual sum of squares exceeds that of the intercept-only model.

title: Theorem 6.7.2
content: Assume \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) and \(\y\notin\spn(\bone)\) . Let \(\theta\) be the angle between the centred response \(\y-\bar y\bone\) and the centred fitted vector \(\hY-\bar y\bone\) . Then \[ R^2=\cos^2\theta=\operatorname{corr}(\y,\hY)^2 , \] where \(\operatorname{corr}\) is the sample correlation. For simple regression on one regressor \(\x\) , \(R^2=\operatorname{corr}(\y,\x)^2\) .

title: Theorem 6.7.1 (Invariance under reparameterization)
content: Let \(\X\) ( \(n\times p\) ) and \(\W\) ( \(n\times q\) ) satisfy \(\C(\X)=\C(\W)\) . Then the two linear models \(\E(\Y)=\X\bbeta\) and \(\E(\Y)=\W\bgamma\) have the same projection \(\M\) , the same fitted values and residuals for every \(\y\) , and the same residual sum of squares. There are a \(p\times q\) matrix \(\bT\) with \(\W=\X\bT\) and a \(q\times p\) matrix \(\bS\) with \(\X=\W\bS\) . If \(\hat{\bgamma}\) is a least squares estimate for \(\W\) , then \(\bT\hat{\bgamma}\) is one for \(\X\) , and \(\bS\hbeta\) is one for \(\W\) whenever \(\hbeta\) is one for \(\X\) . If both matrices have full column rank, then \(p=q\) , \(\bT=\bS^{-1}\) , and \(\hat{\bgamma}=\bS\hbeta\) .

title: Definition 6.8.1 (Leverage)
content: The leverage of observation \(i\) is \(h_{ii}=m_{ii}\) , the \(i\) th diagonal entry of \(\M\) . In this context \(\M\) is often called the hat matrix and written \(\bH\) , because it “puts the hat on” \(\y\) .

title: Example (High-leverage states)
content: Return to the state data, now with all \(51\) jurisdictions including the District of Columbia, and the model of @exm-proj-fwl-crime . The average leverage is \(p/n=0.078\) , and the smallest is \(0.021\) , just above the bound \(1/n\) . The three largest are Jurisdiction \(h_{ii}\) multiple of average District of Columbia 0.506 6.5 Mississippi 0.212 2.7 Alaska 0.177 2.3 The District of Columbia is entirely urban, with by far the highest proportion of single-parent households. It sits at a corner of the regressor cloud that no state comes near, and its leverage is about half the maximum possible. It was omitted from @exm-proj-fwl-crime . @exr-proj-dc asks what happens to the poverty coefficient when it is put back.

title: Exercise (B2)
content: Show that adding a column to \(\X\) cannot decrease any leverage. Show that the leverages in a one-way layout are \(1/n_k\) for members of group \(k\) , and explain why an observation forming a group on its own has leverage one.

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Show that \(m_{ij}^2\le m_{ii}(1-m_{ii})\) for \(i\neq j\) , and hence \(\lvert m_{ij}\rvert\le1/2\) . When is the bound attained?

title: Exercise (A1)
content: For simple regression, derive \(h_{ii}=n^{-1}+(x_i-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}\) directly from @exm-proj-simple-nested , and show that the largest leverage belongs to the observation with \(x_i\) farthest from \(\bar x\) .

title: Proposition 6.8.1 (Properties of leverage)
content: Let \(\rank(\X)=r\) , and let \(\vect{e}_i\) denote the \(i\) th standard basis vector. Then: \(h_{ii}=\norm{\M\vect{e}_i}^2=\sum_j m_{ij}^2\) , the squared length of the projection of \(\vect{e}_i\) onto \(\C(\X)\) ; \(0\le h_{ii}\le1\) , and \(\sum_i h_{ii}=r\) , so the average leverage is \(r/n\) ; if \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) , then \(h_{ii}\ge1/n\) ; \(h_{ii}=1\) iff \(\vect{e}_i\in\C(\X)\) . In that case \(\hat y_i=y_i\) for every \(\y\) , the \(i\) th residual is always zero, and \(m_{ij}=0\) for \(j\ne i\) ; if \(\X=\Q\R\) with \(\Q\) having orthonormal columns spanning \(\C(\X)\) , then \(h_{ii}\) is the squared length of the \(i\) th row of \(\Q\) .

title: Proposition 6.8.2
content: Under these assumptions, \[ h_{ii}=\frac1n+(\x_{(i)}-\bar{\x})\T\bigl(\tilde{\X}_1\T\tilde{\X}_1\bigr)^{-1}(\x_{(i)}-\bar{\x}), \] where \(\x_{(i)}\) is the \(i\) th row of \(\X_1\) , written as a column vector.

title: Definition 6.9.1 (Generalized least squares)
content: A generalized least squares (GLS) estimate minimizes \((\y-\X\bb)\T\V^{-1}(\y-\X\bb)\) . Equivalently, \(\X\hbeta_{\text{GLS}}=\bP_{\X,\V^{-1}}\y\) , and \(\hbeta_{\text{GLS}}\) solves the generalized normal equations \(\X\T\V^{-1}\X\bb=\X\T\V^{-1}\y\) .

title: Example (Autocorrelated errors)
content: Take eight equally spaced observations with a linear trend and error covariance \(v_{st}=0.7^{\lvert s-t\rvert}\) . The \(\V^{-1}\) -projection onto \(\C(\X)\) is idempotent and self-adjoint for \(\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_{\V^{-1}}\) but not symmetric: its largest asymmetry \(\max\lvert p_{st}-p_{ts}\rvert\) is \(0.444\) . The ordinary and generalized slope estimates are \(0.648\) and \(0.650\) . The listing checks each claim, including that the GLS fit is ordinary least squares on whitened data.

title: Example (Engel’s food expenditure data)
content: Engel’s 1857 survey of \(235\) Belgian working-class households records annual income and food expenditure. The spread of expenditure grows with income, as Figure 6.9.1 (a) shows. Weighting by \(w_i=1/\text{income}_i^2\) (standard deviation proportional to income) changes the fitted slope from \(0.4852\) to \(0.5740\) . The change in geometry shows up more clearly in the leverages, panel (b). Under ordinary least squares the richest households have the most leverage, with a maximum of \(0.255\) . In the weighted geometry their large variance shrinks their influence, and no household has leverage above \(0.037\) . Whether this is the right geometry depends on whether the variance model holds. Chapter 21 discusses how to check it, and how to get valid standard errors when it fails.

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Let \(\V=(1-\rho)\I+\rho\bone\bone\T\) with \(-1/(n-1)<\rho<1\) . Show that \(\V\) is positive definite and that \(\C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X)\) whenever \(\bone\in\C(\X)\) . Conclude that ordinary least squares is generalized least squares for equicorrelated errors in any model with an intercept.

title: Exercise (B1)
content: Complete the proof of @thm-proj-A-projection . Show that \(\bP_{\X,\A}\) is symmetric iff it equals \(\M\) , and deduce from @thm-proj-kruskal (with \(\V=\A^{-1}\) ) that this happens iff \(\A\C(\X)\subseteq\C(\X)\) .

title: Exercise (B2)
Exercise (B3)
content: For weighted least squares, \(\V=\diag(1/w_1,\dots,1/w_n)\) with \(w_i>0\) . Show that the diagonal entries of \(\bP_{\X,\V^{-1}}\) equal those of the orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\bm W^{1/2}\X)\) , where \(\bm W=\diag(w_i)\) , and that they sum to \(\rank(\X)\) . Interpret them as leverages.

title: Proposition 6.9.2
content: An idempotent matrix \(\bP\) is the \(\A\) -orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\bP)\) iff \(\A\bP\) is symmetric, that is, iff \(\inner{\bP\bu}{\bv}_{\A}=\inner{\bu}{\bP\bv}_{\A}\) for all \(\bu,\bv\) .

title: Proposition 6.9.4
content: Let \(\bP\) be idempotent. Then \(\Real^n=\C(\bP)\dirsum\Null(\bP)\) , and \(\bP\) maps each \(\y=\bu+\bv\) ( \(\bu\in\C(\bP)\) , \(\bv\in\Null(\bP)\) ) to \(\bu\) . Conversely, for any decomposition \(\Real^n=\mathcal S\dirsum\mathcal T\) there is exactly one idempotent \(\bP\) with \(\C(\bP)=\mathcal S\) and \(\Null(\bP)=\mathcal T\) , the projection onto \(\mathcal S\) along \(\mathcal T\) . It is an orthogonal projection iff \(\mathcal T=\mathcal S\perpc\) , that is, iff \(\bP\) is symmetric.

title: Theorem 6.9.1
content: Let \(\A\) be positive definite and \(\X\) any \(n\times p\) matrix. The \(\A\) -orthogonal projection onto \(\C(\X)\) is \[ \bP_{\X,\A}=\X(\X\T\A\X)\ginv\X\T\A, \] for any generalized inverse. It satisfies \(\bP_{\X,\A}^2=\bP_{\X,\A}\) and \(\C(\bP_{\X,\A})=\C(\X)\) , and the matrix \(\A\bP_{\X,\A}\) is symmetric. The matrix \(\bP_{\X,\A}\) itself is symmetric iff \(\A\C(\X)\subseteq\C(\X)\) , and in general it is not.

title: Theorem 6.9.3 (Kruskal)
content: For positive definite \(\V\) , \(\M\y=\bP_{\X,\V^{-1}}\y\) for every \(\y\) iff \(\C(\V\X)\subseteq\C(\X)\) .

title: Example (Polynomial regression)
content: The columns \(1,t,t^2,\dots,t^d\) evaluated at 200 equally spaced points in \([0,1]\) become nearly dependent as \(d\) grows. To isolate the numerical error, the listing sets \(\y=\X\bbeta\) exactly for a random \(\bbeta\) , so that the true least squares solution is \(\bbeta\) itself. For \(d=8\) the condition number is \(6.8\times 10^{5}\) . The normal equations return \(\bbeta\) with relative error \(1.0\times 10^{-5}\) , while QR achieves \(1.7\times 10^{-11}\) . At \(d=13\) , with \(\kappa(\X)=4.1\times 10^{9}\) , the normal-equation answer has relative error \(9.3\times 10^{-1}\) and not one correct digit, while QR still gets \(4.4\times 10^{-9}\) . Figure 6.10.1 plots the whole sequence against the reference lines \(\kappa\epsilon\) and \(\kappa^2\epsilon\) , where \(\epsilon\approx2.2\times10^{-16}\) is machine precision.

title: Exercise (C1)
content: Let \(\X=[\bone,\x]\) with \(\bar x=c\) and \(S_{xx}=s^2 n\) . Find \(\kappa(\X)\) as a function of \(c\) , \(s\) and \(n\) , and show that it grows without bound as \(c\to\infty\) with \(s\) fixed. Show that centring the regressor, a reparameterization, reduces the condition number to \(\max(1,s)/\min(1,s)\) .

title: Proposition 6.10.1 (Minimum-norm least squares)
content: \(\hbeta^+=\X^+\y\) is a least squares estimate, and it has the smallest Euclidean norm among all least squares estimates.

title: Definition 6.11.1 (Best linear predictor)
page: 6.11 Projection in the population: best linear prediction
content: The best linear predictor of \(Y\) given \(\bm X\) , written \(L(Y\mid\bm X)\) , is the projection of \(Y\) onto \(\mathcal L\) . It is the \(a+\bb\T\bm X\) that minimizes the mean squared error \(\E(Y-a-\bb\T\bm X)^2\) .

title: Example (A curved mean)
page: 6.11 Projection in the population: best linear prediction
content: Let \(X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,2)\) and \(Y=e^X+\varepsilon\) with independent \(\varepsilon\sim\Normal(0,0.25)\) . The regression function is not linear, but @thm-proj-blp still identifies a best line. A short calculation gives \(\Cov(X,Y)=1\) and \(\Var(X)=1/3\) , so the population projection has slope \(3.000\) and intercept \(0.195\) . The listing fits least squares lines to samples of increasing size. The estimates settle on these values, not on any feature of \(e^x\) . Figure 6.11.1 shows the regression function, the population projection, and a least squares fit.

title: Proposition 6.11.2
page: 6.11 Projection in the population: best linear prediction
content: Let \(m(\bm X)=\E(Y\mid\bm X)\) with \(\E Y^2<\infty\) . Then: \(m(\bm X)\) is the projection of \(Y\) onto \(\mathcal G\) . It minimizes \(\E\bigl(Y-g(\bm X)\bigr)^2\) over \(g\) , and \(\E\bigl[(Y-m(\bm X))g(\bm X)\bigr]=0\) for all \(g(\bm X)\in\mathcal G\) ; \(L(Y\mid\bm X)=L\bigl(m(\bm X)\mid\bm X\bigr)\) : the best linear predictor of \(Y\) equals the best linear predictor of the regression function; \(\E\bigl(Y-L(Y\mid\bm X)\bigr)^2=\E\bigl(Y-m(\bm X)\bigr)^2 +\E\bigl(m(\bm X)-L(Y\mid\bm X)\bigr)^2\) ; if \(m\) is affine, \(m(\bm X)=L(Y\mid\bm X)\) .

title: Proposition 6.11.3 (Consistency for the projection)
page: 6.11 Projection in the population: best linear prediction
content: Let \((\bm X_i,Y_i)\) , \(i=1,2,\dots\) , be independent copies of \((\bm X,Y)\) with finite second moments and \(\bSigma_{XX}\) positive definite. Let \((\hat{\alpha}_n,\hbeta_n)\) be the least squares coefficients from the first \(n\) observations, with an intercept. Then \((\hat{\alpha}_n,\hbeta_n)\to(\alpha^*,\bbeta^*)\) with probability one. No assumption about the form of \(\E(Y\mid\bm X)\) , the distribution of the errors, or their variance is needed.

title: Theorem 6.11.1
page: 6.11 Projection in the population: best linear prediction
content: Let \(\bmu_X=\E\bm X\) , \(\mu_Y=\E Y\) , \(\bSigma_{XX}=\Cov(\bm X)\) and \(\bm\sigma_{XY}=\Cov(\bm X,Y)\) , and suppose \(\bSigma_{XX}\) is positive definite. Then \[ L(Y\mid\bm X)=\alpha^*+\bbeta^{*\top}\bm X, \qquad \bbeta^*=\bSigma_{XX}^{-1}\bm\sigma_{XY}, \qquad \alpha^*=\mu_Y-\bbeta^{*\top}\bmu_X . \] The prediction error \(U=Y-L(Y\mid\bm X)\) has mean zero and is uncorrelated with every component of \(\bm X\) . Moreover \[ \Var(Y)=\Var\bigl(L(Y\mid\bm X)\bigr)+\E U^2, \qquad \frac{\Var\bigl(L(Y\mid\bm X)\bigr)}{\Var(Y)} =\frac{\bm\sigma_{XY}\T\bSigma_{XX}^{-1}\bm\sigma_{XY}}{\Var(Y)} . \] {#eq-proj-population-pythagoras}
